subject: system-design
title: Fundamentals
summary: The core vocabulary and reasoning tools of system design: requirements, latency, availability, scalability, estimation, CAP/PACELC and trade-offs.

lessons.title: Turn features into measurable requirements
lessons.summary: Distinguish observable features from numerical service targets, and let each request path have its own priorities.
lessons.body:
System design is the work of deciding *which components a system has, how they talk to each other, and where data lives*, so that the system does what users need at the scale, speed, cost and reliability the business needs.

Writing code answers "how does this function work?". System design answers bigger questions. Where does a request go first? What happens when a machine dies? How much will this cost when traffic grows ten times?

There is rarely one right answer. A good design is one whose trade-offs are **explicit and suited to the requirements**. That is why every good design starts with requirements, not boxes and arrows.

## Why requirements come first

Imagine two teams asked to "build a URL shortener".

- Team A builds for 100 internal users. A single Postgres instance and a small web app is perfect.
- Team B builds for a public service with 100 million new links and 10 billion redirects a month. They need capacity and failure-mode analysis; caching, partitioning or multiple regions may be justified by measured bottlenecks and availability/latency requirements, not traffic totals alone.

Same feature list, completely different systems. The difference is entirely in the **non-functional requirements** and **constraints**. If you skip them, you'll either over-engineer (wasting months) or under-engineer (falling over on launch day).

## Functional requirements

Functional requirements describe **what the system does**: the behaviours a user or another system can observe.

For a URL shortener:

- Given a long URL, return a short code.
- Visiting `/abc123` redirects to the original URL.
- Optionally: custom aliases, expiry dates, click analytics.

A useful habit is to write them as user stories or API calls:

```
POST /links  {url}      -> {code}
GET  /{code}            -> 301/302
GET  /links/{code}/stats -> {clicks}
```

Then **prioritise**. In an interview or a real project kickoff, agree which features are in scope for the first version. "Analytics is nice-to-have; the redirect path is the core."

Even a tiny API line hides decisions that features drive. A `301 Moved Permanently` is heuristically cacheable, so some repeat visits may bypass your servers. A `302 Found` or `307` is not heuristically cacheable, but explicit freshness headers can still permit caching. Set an appropriate cache policy (for example `Cache-Control: no-store`) when each redirect must reach the service for analytics. If click analytics is in scope, that requirement quietly decides the status code and multiplies your redirect traffic.

## Non-functional requirements

Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe **how well** the system does those things. They are the "-ilities", and they drive most architectural decisions.

| NFR | Example target |
|---|---|
| Latency | Redirect p99 < 50 ms |
| Throughput | 100k redirects/s peak |
| Availability | 99.99% for redirects |
| Durability | Never lose a created link |
| Consistency | New link usable within 1 s |
| Scalability | 10x growth in 3 years |
| Security | Block malware URLs |
| Cost | < £5k/month infra |

Notice the targets are **numbers**. "Fast" and "highly available" are useless because nobody can test them. "p99 under 50 ms" can be measured, alerted on and designed for.

> [!tip] Make NFRs differ per path
> Different parts of a system deserve different targets. The redirect path in a URL shortener must be very fast and very available. The analytics dashboard can be slower and eventually consistent. Saying this out loud is a sign of seniority.

## Key takeaways
- Clarify what the system does before choosing technologies.
- Replace “fast” and “available” with measurable targets, separately for each path.
- Redirect analytics depend on cache policy as well as the HTTP status code.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)
- [HTTP semantics (RFC 9110)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html)

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app already lets users upload and follow others, but users complain its feed feels slow. Which requirement gives the team a measurable performance goal?

options.text: The home feed loads with p99 latency under 300 ms
options.explanation: Correct. This describes how well the system performs a function (latency), and it is measurable, which is exactly what a good non-functional requirement looks like.

options.text: Users can follow other users
options.explanation: Incorrect. Following is a feature, i.e. a functional requirement. It says nothing about speed, availability or scale.

options.text: Users can upload a photo with a caption
options.explanation: Incorrect. This describes a behaviour the user can observe (what the system does), so it is a functional requirement.

options.text: Users can delete their own photos
options.explanation: Incorrect. Deletion is a capability of the system, so it is functional. A related NFR might be 'deleted photos are purged from all caches within 24 hours'.

questions.workedExample: The missing goal concerns how well an existing feature performs. A latency percentile plus a threshold gives something the team can measure under a defined workload and observation window. Uploading, following and deleting are behaviours; they do not specify the feed's performance.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says: "Design a URL shortener." What should you do **first**?

options.text: Draw the load balancer, app servers and database
options.explanation: Incorrect. Drawing boxes before knowing scale and requirements means you can't justify any of them; you may design something massively over- or under-sized.

options.text: Write the code for base-62 encoding
options.explanation: Incorrect. Encoding is a detail for the deep-dive stage. Starting there skips requirements, estimation and the high-level design.

options.text: Choose a database, e.g. Cassandra for scale
options.explanation: Incorrect. Picking a technology before knowing the requirements is the classic 'jumping to technology' mistake. Cassandra might be wildly unnecessary for a small internal tool.

options.text: Ask clarifying questions about features, scale and non-functional targets
options.explanation: Correct. Requirements (features, expected traffic, latency and availability targets, constraints) determine every later decision, so clarifying them is the first step.

questions.workedExample:
The standard sequence is:

1. Clarify requirements (functional, non-functional, constraints)
2. Estimate scale
3. API and data model
4. High-level design
5. Deep dives
6. Bottlenecks and trade-offs

For a URL shortener, clarifying might reveal: 100M new links/month, 100:1 read:write ratio, redirects must be very fast and highly available, links never expire. Those answers drive caching, storage and ID-generation choices later.

questions.prompt: A product manager states the requirement: "The system must be highly available and fast." What is the main problem with this requirement?

options.text: Availability and speed are functional requirements, not non-functional
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability and latency are classic non-functional requirements. The categorisation is fine; the wording is the problem.

options.text: You can't have both high availability and low latency
options.explanation: Incorrect. Many systems achieve both. There are trade-offs (PACELC describes latency vs consistency), but availability and speed are not mutually exclusive.

options.text: It isn't measurable, so it can't drive design decisions or be verified
options.explanation: Correct. Without numbers (e.g. 99.95% monthly availability, p99 < 200 ms) you can't decide whether you need multi-region failover or a cache, and you can't test whether you've succeeded.

options.text: Availability should only be specified by the infrastructure team
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability targets are a business decision based on the cost of downtime; product owners should be involved in setting them.

questions.workedExample: Replace each vague adjective with a target and measurement definition. For example, specify the share of checkout requests that must succeed over 30 days, and the page-load percentile at an agreed peak workload. Then inspect whether measured database latency, recovery times and dependency failures fit those budgets. A particular target does not automatically prescribe a cache or multi-zone design; evidence and failure assumptions decide that.

questions.prompt: In a URL shortener, the redirect path must be 99.99% available, while the click-analytics dashboard is only 99.5%. Which design consequence follows most directly from setting **different** targets per path?

options.text: Both paths must share the same database so they stay consistent
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sharing a database couples their availability: a heavy analytics query could degrade redirects. Different targets argue for separation, not sharing.

options.text: The analytics dashboard needs multi-region active-active deployment
options.explanation: Incorrect. A lower dashboard target does not itself justify multi-region active-active deployment. Choose its recovery design from the actual business impact and failure model.

options.text: Analytics events should be recorded asynchronously so analytics failures can't block redirects
options.explanation: Correct. If the redirect handler synchronously writes click data to the analytics store, the redirect's availability is capped by the analytics store's. Emitting events to a queue or log decouples them, so the 99.5% component can't drag down the 99.99% path.

options.text: Redirects should be served from the analytics store to reduce duplication
options.explanation: Incorrect. This puts the critical path on the less reliable component, which is exactly backwards.

questions.workedExample: Trace which components must succeed before a redirect can respond. If analytics must acknowledge a synchronous write, an analytics outage blocks redirects even while the link store is healthy. Move optional analytics processing off that path, and decide whether events may be dropped or must be durably buffered. Any required queue acknowledgement is still a dependency; asynchronous processing alone does not remove it.

questions.prompt: Your URL shortener must report accurate click counts per link. A colleague wants redirects to return `301 Moved Permanently` "because it's the correct status for a permanent link". What is the main problem?

options.text: Browsers may cache a 301, so repeat clicks never reach your servers and go uncounted
options.explanation: Correct. A 301 is cacheable by default, so a browser that has seen it can redirect locally next time. That saves you load but silently breaks the click-analytics requirement. A 302 or 307 can also be cached when explicit freshness permits it; set a suitable policy such as `Cache-Control: no-store` if each request must reach the service.

options.text: A 301 is slower for users than a 302
options.explanation: Incorrect. On the first visit both cost one round trip. A cached 301 is actually faster for repeat visits, which is exactly why it hides clicks from you.

options.text: Search engines ignore 301 redirects
options.explanation: Incorrect. Search engines follow 301s and treat them as permanent moves. SEO isn't the issue; analytics accuracy is.

options.text: A 301 cannot carry a `Location` header
options.explanation: Incorrect. Both 301 and 302 use the `Location` header to name the target URL.

questions.workedExample:
Trace a user clicking the same short link twice:

```
301: click 1 -> server -> counted
     click 2 -> browser cache -> lost
302: click 1 -> server -> counted
     click 2 -> server -> counted
```

The analytics requirement shapes both redirect semantics and cache policy. The 302 trace assumes caching is prohibited (for example with `Cache-Control: no-store`); status 302 alone does not guarantee every click reaches the server.

lessons.title: Scope a design around constraints and load
lessons.summary: Use team, budget, regulation and traffic assumptions to rule out unsuitable architectures before drawing them.
lessons.body:
Requirements set the goal; constraints set the limits within which the team must achieve it. Traffic assumptions connect that goal to a practical capacity plan.

## Constraints

Constraints are things you **can't change** (or can't change cheaply):

- **Team**: three engineers who know Python and Postgres.
- **Time**: must launch in four months.
- **Budget**: fixed cloud spend.
- **Regulation**: payment card data falls under PCI DSS; GDPR requires safeguards for transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area; an organisation may additionally require EU-only residency. Such a residency rule is a specified policy, not a universal GDPR requirement.
- **Existing systems**: must integrate with the company's identity provider.

Constraints often rule out "textbook" answers. A team of three probably shouldn't run its own Kafka cluster and Cassandra ring; managed services are usually the right call.

## Assumptions and scale

Next, establish the numbers the design must support:

- Daily active users (DAU), and how many actions each performs.
- Read-to-write ratio (a URL shortener might be 100:1).
- Data size per item and retention period.
- Peak versus average load (a 2–10x factor is an illustrative planning range, not a universal statistic; measure the traffic shape).

You'll turn these into queries per second, storage and bandwidth in the estimation lesson. The point here is that **you can't choose components without them**. A Postgres primary's sustainable write rate depends on hardware, schema, batching, durability and contention. Benchmark the intended workload before treating a guessed rate as a capacity limit.

The read-to-write ratio is especially telling. At 100:1, almost all the work is reads, so caching and read replicas pay off and the write path can stay simple. A write-heavy system (logging, metrics, chat) pushes you towards partitioning writes and append-friendly storage instead.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Jumping to technology
> "We'll use Kafka, Redis and Kubernetes" before knowing the requirements is the most common failure. Technology choices should be *conclusions*, justified by requirements.

- **Designing for imaginary scale.** Planning for a billion users when you have a thousand adds cost and complexity with no benefit. Design for roughly 10x your expected load and know how you'd get to 100x.
- **Ignoring failure.** Every component fails eventually. For each box, ask "what happens when this is down or slow?"
- **Unquantified NFRs.** "It should be fast" can't drive a decision.
- **Ignoring operations.** Who deploys it, monitors it and gets paged at 3 a.m.? A design the team can't operate is a bad design.
- **One-size consistency.** Not everything needs strong consistency; not everything can tolerate eventual consistency. Decide per data type.

## Key takeaways
- Constraints narrow the feasible design: team, time, budget, regulation and existing systems matter.
- Estimate behaviour, read/write balance, retained data and peak load before choosing components.
- Avoid imaginary scale, unmeasurable goals and systems the team cannot operate.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)
- [European Commission: international transfers](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/rules-international-data-transfers_en)

questions.prompt: Which of the following are **constraints** rather than requirements? Select all that apply.

options.text: The team of four engineers only knows Java and MySQL
options.explanation: Correct. Team skills are a fixed condition you must design around, not something the system should achieve.

options.text: EU customer data must remain in EU regions
options.explanation: Correct. This is a regulatory or policy constraint. GDPR regulates transfers to third countries, allowing them under applicable mechanisms such as adequacy decisions or safeguards; an EU-only residency rule can be an additional organisational policy. You don't choose it; it limits your options, such as which regions you replicate to.

options.text: Checkout p99 latency must be under 500 ms
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a non-functional requirement: a target the system must meet, not an external limitation.

options.text: Launch must happen within three months
options.explanation: Correct. A deadline is a time constraint. It pushes you towards managed services and simpler designs.

options.text: Users can reset their password by email
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a functional requirement: a behaviour of the system.

questions.workedExample:
Sort each item into one of three buckets:

| Item | Bucket |
|---|---|
| Team knows Java/MySQL | Constraint (people) |
| EU data stays in EU | Constraint (specified residency policy) |
| Checkout p99 < 500 ms | Non-functional requirement |
| Launch in 3 months | Constraint (time) |
| Password reset | Functional requirement |

Requirements describe what the system must do or achieve. Constraints are conditions imposed from outside that limit how you can achieve it.

questions.prompt: A start-up with three engineers and a six-month runway asks you to design an MVP marketplace expecting ~50 orders per minute at launch. A senior engineer proposes microservices on self-managed Kubernetes, Kafka and Cassandra "so we never have to re-architect". What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Cassandra can't handle 50 orders per minute
options.explanation: Incorrect. Cassandra can handle vastly more than that. The problem isn't capacity; it's that the capacity is unnecessary.

options.text: Kafka loses messages, so orders would be lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. Kafka with replication, `acks=all` and a sensible `min.insync.replicas` is durable. Message loss isn't the core objection.

options.text: Microservices are always worse than monoliths
options.explanation: Incorrect. Microservices are a valid choice for large organisations with independent teams. 'Always worse' is an overgeneralisation; here they're wrong because of team size and scale.

options.text: The design ignores the team and time constraints: operating it would consume the team, for scale they don't need
options.explanation: Correct. The team must operate every chosen component while building an MVP. At the stated launch load, a simpler managed design is a candidate to benchmark before taking on several specialist systems.

questions.workedExample: Start with the team, deadline and actual transaction workload. Each proposed infrastructure component adds deployment, upgrades, monitoring and recovery work. A modular application with a managed database is a candidate that preserves scarce engineering time. Benchmark its transaction and failure behaviour, document growth triggers, and add complexity when a concrete requirement justifies it.

questions.prompt: You have five minutes to clarify a "design a URL shortener" brief. Which questions are most likely to **change the architecture**? Select all that apply.

options.text: How many redirects per second at peak, and how many new links per day?
options.explanation: Correct. Scale decides whether one database suffices or you need caching, replicas and partitioning.

options.text: What colour should the shorten button be?
options.explanation: Incorrect. UI styling has no effect on components, data placement or scaling.

options.text: Do we need per-link click analytics, and how fresh must it be?
options.explanation: Correct. Analytics adds a high-volume write stream, affects the redirect status code, and freshness decides between a batch pipeline and a streaming one.

options.text: Do links ever expire, and can users choose custom aliases?
options.explanation: Correct. Expiry affects retention and storage growth; custom aliases need uniqueness checks and change how codes are generated.

options.text: Should the code use tabs or spaces?
options.explanation: Incorrect. Code style is irrelevant to system design.

questions.workedExample:
For each question, ask: *would a different answer change a box, an arrow or a data store?*

| Question | Changes design? |
|---|---|
| Peak QPS, links/day | Yes: caching, sharding |
| Button colour | No |
| Analytics, freshness | Yes: event pipeline |
| Expiry, aliases | Yes: storage, ID scheme |
| Tabs vs spaces | No |

Good clarifying questions target scale, features with architectural weight, and non-functional targets.

lessons.title: Walk a request and challenge its failure modes
lessons.summary: Build a simple architecture, trace the critical path, and use cache failure and ticket inventory to expose hidden risks.
lessons.body:
Once the requirements and scale are clear, start with the simplest architecture that meets them. Trace a real request, then ask what happens when a component disappears or becomes slow.

## A repeatable approach

Most practitioners use some variant of this sequence:

```
1. Clarify requirements
   functional / non-functional / constraints
2. Estimate scale
   QPS, storage, bandwidth
3. Define the API and data model
4. High-level design
   boxes, arrows, request flow
5. Deep dive on the hard parts
   hot keys, consistency, failure
6. Identify bottlenecks and trade-offs
   what breaks first, what you'd change
```

### Step 4: the high-level design

Start with the simplest thing that meets the requirements, then evolve it.

```
 client
   |
   v
+--------+    +-----------+    +--------+
|  load  |--->|  app tier |--->|   DB   |
|balancer|    | stateless |    |primary |
+--------+    +-----------+    +--------+
                    |              |
                    v              v
                 +-----+      +--------+
                 |cache|      |replicas|
                 +-----+      +--------+
```

Walk a request through it: "A redirect hits the load balancer, goes to any app server, checks the cache, falls back to a read replica on a miss." Walking the flow catches missing pieces quickly.

### Step 5: deep dives

This is where the real design happens. Pick the parts that are hard *for this system*:

- How are short codes generated without collisions across many servers?
- What happens if the cache cluster fails?
- What's the hot-key story when one link goes viral?

The cache question decides whether the cache is an optimisation or critical infrastructure. The database normally sees only cache misses. At a 95% hit rate and 100,000 reads/s, it sees 5,000 reads/s. If the cache disappears and every miss falls through, it sees all 100,000 reads/s: twenty times its normal load.

Can the database survive that jump? If not, plan admission control, bounded retries and a degraded response instead of allowing every request to fall through. This example assumes one database read per miss; retries can make an outage worse.

Later modules cover the tools for these questions: caching, databases and partitioning, consistency and consensus, messaging, API design and reliability patterns.

## A worked mini-example

> [!example] "Design a ticket-booking system for concerts"
> **Functional:** browse events, hold seats for 10 minutes, pay, receive ticket.
>
> **Non-functional:** never sell the same seat twice (strong consistency on seat state); browse page p99 < 200 ms; survive a 50x traffic spike when a big tour goes on sale.
>
> **Constraints:** payments via an existing provider; 6 engineers; launch in 6 months.
>
> **Implications:** seat inventory needs transactions or conditional writes; the browse path can be heavily cached; the on-sale spike suggests a virtual waiting room or queue in front of checkout. Already the architecture is taking shape, and we haven't drawn a single box.

## Key takeaways
- Follow requirements, estimates, APIs, request flow, deep dives and explicit trade-offs.
- A cache at 95% hit rate hides a potential 20-fold database load increase when it fails.
- Ticket inventory needs concurrency-safe decisions; browse caching and a waiting room serve different goals.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: You're designing a concert ticketing system. Which requirement should most strongly shape how you store **seat inventory**?

options.text: Each seat must never be sold to two people
options.explanation: Correct. This is a strong consistency requirement on seat state. It points to transactions, conditional writes or a single authoritative owner per seat, rather than an eventually consistent store.

options.text: The event browse page must load in under 200 ms
options.explanation: Incorrect. Browse latency is best handled by caching event pages. It doesn't dictate how authoritative seat state is stored.

options.text: Users can view their past orders
options.explanation: Incorrect. Order history is a read-mostly feature that can tolerate some staleness; it doesn't drive seat inventory storage.

options.text: Ticket PDFs must be emailed within 5 minutes
options.explanation: Incorrect. This suggests an asynchronous queue for email sending, but it's independent of how seat state is stored.

questions.workedExample:
Map each requirement to the component it affects:

1. Browse latency -> cache / CDN for event pages.
2. No double-selling -> seat inventory storage. You need an atomic 'reserve if free' operation, e.g. `UPDATE seats SET holder=? WHERE id=? AND holder IS NULL` in Postgres, or a DynamoDB conditional write.
3. Order history -> read replica or secondary store.
4. Email within 5 min -> background queue and worker.

The requirement with the strictest correctness guarantee (no double sale) determines the inventory store's design.

questions.prompt: A redirect service peaks at 100,000 reads/s with a 95% cache hit rate. The read replicas are sized for 8,000 reads/s. During the deep dive you ask "what if the cache cluster fails?" What is the right conclusion?

options.text: Nothing to worry about: the replicas already have 60% headroom over normal miss traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect. The headroom is over the *miss* traffic only. With no cache, every read becomes a miss.

options.text: Cache loss sends the full read load to replicas that cannot handle it; plan capacity, admission control or a degraded response
options.explanation: Correct. The database normally receives only misses. With the cache gone, all 100,000 reads/s can reach replicas sized for 8,000 reads/s.

options.text: The databases would see about 10,000 reads/s, a modest overload
options.explanation: Incorrect. This underestimates the load: losing the cache sends all 100k reads to the database, not double the miss traffic.

options.text: Redirects would get slower but would all still succeed
options.explanation: Incorrect. At 12.5x overload, queues grow without bound and requests time out. Overload causes failures, not just slowness.

questions.workedExample: Compare request paths. A cache hit ends without a database read; a miss reaches a replica. Removing the cache turns every request into a miss, so ordinary miss-traffic headroom is irrelevant. Treat the cache as critical infrastructure if the database cannot survive its loss. Spread cache failures, coalesce repeated misses, bound retries and shed excess work before it overloads the replicas.

questions.prompt: In a concert ticketing system, which pieces of data most clearly need authoritative, concurrency-safe decisions on the checkout path (while display reads may still be cached)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Which user currently holds or owns each seat
options.explanation: Correct. A stale value used in an unprotected reservation decision can let two people buy the same seat, which breaks the core 'never double-sell' requirement.

options.text: The "about 200 seats left" banner on the event page
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a display hint. Being a few seconds stale is harmless, so it can be cached or computed asynchronously.

options.text: Whether an order has been paid
options.explanation: Correct. Issuing a ticket for an unpaid order, or charging twice because an order looked unpaid, costs real money. Payment state must be authoritative.

options.text: The artist biography and venue photos
options.explanation: Incorrect. Static content changes rarely and can be served from a CDN with long cache lifetimes.

options.text: Number of people who viewed the event page today
options.explanation: Incorrect. An approximate, eventually consistent counter is fine for a view count.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each item: *what is the cost if a reader sees an old value?*

| Data | Cost of staleness |
|---|---|
| Seat holder | Double sale |
| Seats-left banner | Slightly wrong hint |
| Payment status | Lost money |
| Artist bio | None |
| View count | None |

Protect authoritative seat and payment transitions with atomic operations, constraints and retry-safe workflows. Even these values can have stale display copies if final checkout decisions revalidate correctly; freshness requirements for other data depend on the product.

questions.prompt: Checkout normally sees 200 requests/s. When a big tour goes on sale, 10,000 users/s try to check out for several minutes. The inventory store uses atomic reserve-if-free operations and can sustain about 2,000 of them per second. Which design best meets "survive the spike and never double-sell"?

options.text: Autoscale the stateless checkout servers to 50x
options.explanation: Incorrect. More app servers just forward more load to the inventory store, which is the real bottleneck at 2,000/s. Autoscaling the wrong tier moves the failure, it doesn't remove it.

options.text: Serve seat availability from an eventually consistent cache and reconcile double sales afterwards
options.explanation: Incorrect. This violates the hard 'never double-sell' requirement. Refunding angry fans after the fact is not reconciliation.

options.text: Put a virtual waiting room in front of checkout that admits users at a rate the inventory store can sustain
options.explanation: Correct. Admission control turns an unbounded spike into a steady flow below 2,000/s. Users wait in a queue (with honest progress feedback) instead of the whole system failing for everyone.

options.text: Return HTTP 503 to every request above 2,000/s and let clients retry immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect. Immediate retries multiply load (a retry storm) and the experience is random and unfair. Shedding load needs backoff or, better, an orderly queue.

questions.workedExample: The inventory store is the measured bottleneck: the incoming spike exceeds its sustainable atomic reservation rate. More app servers cannot increase that rate, and a stale cache cannot authorise a sale safely. A waiting room admits work below the store's limit while keeping the atomic reserve-if-free decision authoritative. Bound the queue and retries, and tell users honestly when demand cannot be served.

lessons.title: Separate latency from bandwidth and capacity
lessons.summary: Identify whether parallel capacity, fewer round trips or a faster link addresses the actual performance limit.
lessons.body:
Two numbers describe the performance of almost any system:

- **Latency**: how long a single operation takes, from request to response. Measured in time (ms, µs).
- **Throughput**: how many operations complete per unit time. Measured in requests/s, MB/s, messages/s.

They are related but not the same thing, and confusing them leads to bad designs.

## The pipe analogy

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: parallel water pipes
> A longer pipe delays the first arriving drop. More pipes can carry more water at once.
>
> **How it maps:** Latency is the travel time; throughput is the amount delivered each second. Parallel servers can add capacity without shortening one request's journey.
>
> **Where it stops:** Networks carry packets and servers queue work; their delays depend on contention and processing as well as distance.

```
 latency: travel time along the pipe
 throughput: flow per second

 in  ==============================  out
     <---------- 100 ms ---------->
         carries 1,000 req/s
```

You can increase throughput by adding servers without shortening a lightly loaded request. For an illustrative London–New York link, assume a 70 ms round trip. A signal still has to travel there and back; adding servers cannot remove that propagation delay. Moving work closer or avoiding an exchange can help.

## Bandwidth-bound or latency-bound?

The pipe analogy gives a simple model for how long one transfer takes: a fixed cost for each round trip, plus the time to push the bytes through the pipe.

```formula reference
T ≈ k × RTT + D / B
where
T: the total time for the transfer or exchange, in seconds (s)
k: the number of round trips that must happen one after another (each waits for the previous reply)
RTT: round-trip time, the time for a message to go to the other end and a reply to come back, in s
D: the amount of data to send, in bits (multiply bytes by 8)
B: the bandwidth of the link, in bits per second (bps)
≈: approximately equal to; the model ignores server processing time and protocol overhead
In words: transfer time includes the round trips that must finish one after another, plus the time needed to send all the data at the available bandwidth.
```

For example, under this simplified model a 1 MB file over a 100 Mbps link with one 70 ms round trip takes about 150 ms. Sending the bytes and waiting for the reply both matter; server processing, protocol overhead and congestion would add more delay.

Big transfers are **bandwidth-bound**: the size term dominates, so a fatter pipe or compression helps. Many small, sequential exchanges are **latency-bound**: the round-trip term dominates, so bandwidth upgrades do nothing and you must cut round trips (batching, parallelism, moving closer).

> [!warning] Throughput limits show up as latency
> Users rarely see "throughput exceeded". They see slow pages and timeouts, because the queue in front of the bottleneck is growing.

## Throughput in practice

Throughput depends on hardware, payload size, schema, batching, persistence, concurrency and the target latency percentile. A 10 Gbps link has a raw signalling rate equivalent to 1.25 GB/s before protocol overhead; that is not an application throughput guarantee.

> [!note] Content gap: verified throughput benchmarks
> Generic per-server rates for web APIs, PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka are omitted. No reproducible workload and hardware configuration was provided for those figures, so they cannot be reliably verified as capacity guidance. Benchmark the intended workload and record its settings before using a rate in a design.

## Key takeaways
- Parallel servers increase throughput capacity without necessarily shortening one lightly loaded request.
- Large transfers are often bandwidth-bound; small sequential exchanges pay repeated round trips.
- Treat raw link speeds and per-server rates as inputs to measurement, not application guarantees.

## Further reading
- [The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf)
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

questions.prompt: You double the number of identical, stateless app servers behind a load balancer. The servers were lightly loaded before, requests divide evenly, and the load balancer and downstream systems have spare capacity. What happens most likely?

options.text: Latency halves and throughput doubles
options.explanation: Incorrect. Adding parallel capacity doesn't make an individual request faster when there was no queueing; each request still does the same work and network hops.

options.text: Nothing changes at all
options.explanation: Incorrect. Capacity (maximum throughput) does increase, even if current traffic doesn't use it yet. You'd see the difference under a load spike.

options.text: Latency halves; throughput stays the same
options.explanation: Incorrect. This confuses the two metrics. Parallelism increases throughput capacity; it doesn't speed up a lightly loaded request.

options.text: Maximum throughput roughly doubles; per-request latency stays about the same
options.explanation: Correct. More servers means more requests can be processed concurrently (wider pipe), but a single request's path is unchanged, so its latency is roughly unchanged when the servers weren't saturated.

questions.workedExample: A single lightly loaded request still performs the same work and network exchanges after more servers are added. Extra servers let more requests run at once, so capacity can rise if downstream systems are not the limit. Latency may improve when adding capacity removes queueing; the question explicitly excludes that starting condition.

questions.prompt: Between London and Virginia (RTT 80 ms, 1 Gbps link) you run two jobs: (1) copy one 10 GB backup file; (2) send 1,000 tiny 1 KB requests **one after another**, each waiting for its reply. Both take about 80 seconds. What would speed each one up?

options.text: Upgrade both to a 10 Gbps link
options.explanation: Incorrect. That helps the backup, which is bandwidth-bound, but the tiny requests spend almost all their time waiting on round trips, which bandwidth doesn't shorten.

options.text: Backup: more bandwidth or compression. Requests: batch them or send them in parallel
options.explanation: Correct. The backup spends most of its time transmitting bytes, while the sequential tiny requests repeatedly wait for replies. Each needs a remedy for its own bottleneck.

options.text: Move both to a lower-latency route
options.explanation: Incorrect. Shaving RTT helps the requests, but the backup's 80 s is almost entirely data transfer time, which a shorter path barely changes.

options.text: Neither can be improved, because both are limited by the speed of light
options.explanation: Incorrect. Only the round-trip part is bounded by physics. The backup is limited by bandwidth, and the requests can avoid paying the round trip 1,000 times.

questions.workedExample: Ask what occupies the elapsed time. The backup is one large stream: faster transmission or fewer bytes can shorten it. The tiny requests send very little data but wait for a separate long round trip each time. Batch them, overlap independent requests, or move the work closer. This simplified comparison ignores processing, protocol overhead and congestion; those must be measured before predicting an exact speed-up.

questions.prompt: A mobile app makes 12 tiny API calls one after another to a distant region. Each waits for the previous reply, server processing is negligible, and traces show network waiting dominates. Which change best addresses the cause?

options.text: Add more app servers in the same distant region
options.explanation: Incorrect. The servers are not the measured bottleneck, and this leaves the sequential long-distance exchanges intact.

options.text: Provide one aggregation endpoint close to the data and return one response to the phone
options.explanation: Correct. This replaces repeated long-distance exchanges with one; internal processing and local exchanges still take time.

options.text: Upgrade the phone's bandwidth without changing the calls
options.explanation: Incorrect. The tiny payloads spend most of their time waiting for replies, not transmitting bytes.

options.text: Raise the client timeout
options.explanation: Incorrect. A longer timeout permits more waiting without shortening any exchange.

questions.workedExample: Trace the dependencies: the phone cannot send the next call until the previous reply arrives. Each call therefore pays the distant round trip. Aggregating near the data pays that long journey once. Parallelising independent calls is another option, but dependent calls need an aggregation or protocol change.

lessons.title: Predict queueing and leave capacity headroom
lessons.summary: Explain why queueing grows near saturation and why spare capacity matters during peaks and failures.
lessons.body:
A server can have enough nominal throughput and still give poor latency because requests spend time waiting. Queueing models explain why capacity planning needs spare room.

## How they interact: queueing

Latency and throughput meet through **queueing**. When requests arrive faster than a server can process them, they wait. Waiting time is latency.

The **M/M/1 queue** assumes Poisson arrivals (independent random arrivals at a constant average rate), exponentially distributed service times, and one server serving one request at a time. The two M letters refer to the model’s memoryless arrival and service assumptions. For that model, queueing theory gives the average time a request spends in the system, waiting plus being served:

```formula reference
ρ = λ / μ
W = S / (1 − ρ)
where
W: the average time a request spends in the system (queueing plus being served), in milliseconds (ms); this is the response time within the modelled system
S: the average service time, the time the server spends actually working on one request when there is no queue, in ms
ρ: rho, the utilisation: the fraction of time the server is busy, from 0 (idle) to just under 1 (always busy)
λ: lambda, the arrival rate, in requests per second (req/s)
μ: mu, the service rate (capacity), the most requests per second the server can complete, equal to 1 / S with S in seconds (a 10 ms service time gives 100 req/s)
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
In words: in this single-server model, average response time rises sharply as spare capacity shrinks. Near full utilisation, a small extra load can cause a large increase in waiting.
```

For a modelled server with a 10 ms mean service time, 80% utilisation gives a 50 ms average response: most of that time is waiting. The table illustrates how quickly waiting grows:

| Utilisation | Latency vs service time |
|---|---|
| 50% | 2x |
| 80% | 5x |
| 90% | 10x |
| 99% | 100x |

This is why systems can appear to "fall off a cliff". As utilisation approaches 100% from below, the M/M/1 steady-state mean queue length diverges; at or above 100% the infinite-buffer model has no stable steady state. Capacity planning needs measured headroom rather than a goal of keeping every resource fully busy.

Real servers aren't exactly M/M/1 (they have many workers, and service times vary differently), and the exact curve depends on arrival/service variability, scheduling and queue limits. Many real systems develop large queues near saturation; a deterministic or admission-controlled system need not follow this curve.

## Little's law: how many requests are in flight

Little's law connects average throughput, time in the system and concurrency in a stable system, where work does not accumulate forever. If requests arrive at the same rate but each stays ten times longer, ten times as many are in flight on average. A slow dependency can therefore exhaust upstream threads or connections even without a traffic spike. The pool-sizing unit gives the reference relationship and discusses its limits.

Headroom must also cover failures. If three equally sized zones normally share the load, losing one pushes its work onto the two survivors. Test that case separately from healthy operation; acceptable normal utilisation alone does not prove the survivors will meet the latency target.

## Key takeaways
- The M/M/1 model’s mean latency grows sharply near saturation; real systems depend on their workload, admission rules and scheduling.
- Little’s law multiplies throughput by time in the system to give average concurrency.
- Check both normal load and survivor capacity during failures; headroom must satisfy each target.

## Further reading
- [Little’s Law (Marc Brooker)](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html)
- [Handling Overload (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- [MIT: basic queueing theory](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-763j-manufacturing-system-and-supply-chain-design-spring-2005/22f4805864deb06eee85acc1601463ba_queueing_note.pdf)

questions.prompt: A worker's mean service time stays unchanged as utilisation rises close to full capacity. Under the M/M/1 model, why can a small further load increase cause a large response-time increase?

options.text: Requests spend much longer waiting for the worker, even though their own service time is unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. As spare capacity shrinks, random arrivals and service times create a sharply growing queue.

options.text: Each request necessarily requires more CPU instructions at higher utilisation
options.explanation: Incorrect. The scenario holds service time constant; waiting is the additional delay.

options.text: Response time must rise in direct proportion to utilisation
options.explanation: Incorrect. Near saturation the model's mean response time grows much more sharply than a proportional change.

options.text: Utilisation cannot affect response time if service time stays constant
options.explanation: Incorrect. Response time includes queueing as well as service.

questions.workedExample: Separate time being served from time waiting. A request arriving behind busy work waits before its own service begins. Near full utilisation, the worker has little spare time to drain that backlog, so small load increases can cause large delays. The M/M/1 result depends on its random-arrival, random-service, single-server assumptions; real systems need measurements and queue limits.

questions.prompt: A service meets its normal peak-utilisation target across three equally sized zones. It must also stay below a separate emergency utilisation limit after losing one zone. What must the capacity review do?

options.text: Check only normal utilisation; healthy headroom proves the outage case
options.explanation: Incorrect. Losing a zone removes capacity and shifts work to survivors.

options.text: Assume autoscaling replaces the lost zone instantly
options.explanation: Incorrect. Scaling has delays and may lack capacity during a regional incident.

options.text: Check the two surviving zones against peak traffic and measured latency at the emergency limit
options.explanation: Correct. Normal and failure conditions are separate constraints, and a utilisation limit alone does not guarantee acceptable latency.

options.text: Require the emergency utilisation limit to equal the normal target in every design
options.explanation: Incorrect. A product can choose different normal and degraded targets, provided they are explicit and validated.

questions.workedExample: List the capacity available with all zones, then with one gone. Check the full peak load against each case and provision for the stricter requirement. If the failure policy allows higher utilisation, test its latency and overload behaviour rather than assuming it is safe.

lessons.title: Measure percentiles without hiding slow requests
lessons.summary: Interpret typical and tail latency, then aggregate and collect measurements correctly across a service.
lessons.body:
A single average can hide the slow experience that matters to users. Percentiles identify positions in the latency distribution, but only if the measurements include the requests and waits you mean to represent.

## Why averages lie: percentiles

Suppose 100 requests take these times: 98 take 10 ms, and 2 take 2,000 ms. The mean adds all durations and divides by the request count. It is 49.8 ms, which describes neither group's experience well.

A **percentile** instead identifies a position after sorting requests from fastest to slowest. Under the nearest-rank convention, p50 picks the 50th request out of these 100 and p99 picks the 99th. Other percentile conventions can interpolate, so state the method when small samples matter.

Applied to our 100 requests:

- Mean: **49.8 ms**
- Median (p50), the 50th value: **10 ms**
- p99, the 99th value: **2,000 ms**

The mean describes no real request. It's five times the typical case and 40 times better than the slow case. That's why we use **percentiles**:

- **p50 (median)**: at least half of requests are at or below this threshold (ties and percentile conventions matter). The "typical" experience.
- **p95, p99**: roughly 95% / 99% of requests are at or below these thresholds. The experience of your unluckiest users.
- **p99.9 and above**: often called the **tail**.

```
 count
  |#
  |##
  |####
  |######
  |########
  |##########__
  |            '''--..___ .  .   .
  +-------------------------------> ms
       p50        p99       p99.9
               <--- the tail --->
```

Latency distributions are almost never normal (bell-shaped). They have a long right tail caused by garbage-collection pauses, cache misses, retransmits, lock contention, noisy neighbours and queueing.

## Measuring percentiles correctly

- **You can't average percentiles.** The mean of 10 servers' p99s is not the fleet's p99. Aggregate raw histograms (e.g. HdrHistogram, Prometheus histograms) and compute percentiles from the combined data.
- **Beware coordinated omission.** A load tester that waits for each response before sending the next under-reports latency when the server stalls, because it stops sending during the stall. `wrk2` corrects for this by recording latency from when each request was scheduled to start, even if its actual transmission is delayed.
- **Measure at the client, too.** Server-side timing misses network and queueing time before your code runs.

## Key takeaways
- The mean, median and tail percentiles describe different parts of the same distribution.
- Combine histograms or observations before calculating a fleet percentile; do not average server percentiles.
- Client timing and tests that account for coordinated omission expose waits a server-only metric may miss.

## Further reading
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
- [Histograms and summaries (Prometheus)](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/)
- [The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf)
- [wrk2: corrected latency measurement](https://github.com/giltene/wrk2)

questions.prompt: Most requests finish in 20 ms, but a small group representing 2% of requests takes 3 seconds. Which report best exposes that slow experience?

options.text: Report only the median because it describes every user's experience
options.explanation: Incorrect. The median can remain fast while a minority experiences very slow responses.

options.text: Average the fast and slow durations without weighting their request counts
options.explanation: Incorrect. That treats the two groups as equally common and still does not expose a tail threshold.

options.text: Report the median and p99 alongside the mean
options.explanation: Correct. The median describes typical requests; p99 lies within this slowest 2%, revealing the tail that the mean can soften.

options.text: Replace all percentiles with the mean
options.explanation: Incorrect. The mean combines durations into one number and can hide how differently requests behave.

questions.workedExample: Sort the requests conceptually. More than half are fast, so the median is fast. The slow group occupies the final 2% of positions, which includes the 99th percentile. A mean between the two durations does not mean any actual request took that long.

questions.prompt: You run 20 API servers. Each reports its own p99 latency every minute, and your dashboard shows the **average of the 20 p99 values** as "fleet p99". One server is badly degraded. What is wrong with this metric?

options.text: Nothing; averaging p99s gives the fleet p99 when servers get equal traffic
options.explanation: Incorrect. Percentiles aren't linear, so they can't be averaged even with equal traffic. The true fleet p99 depends on the combined distribution of all requests.

options.text: It should use the median of the p99s instead of the mean
options.explanation: Incorrect. The median of p99s would hide the degraded server even more effectively. Any statistic computed over per-server percentiles is still not the fleet percentile.

options.text: p99 is the wrong metric; use the mean, which can be averaged
options.explanation: Incorrect. Means can be combined, but they hide tail latency, which is the thing you need to see here. The fix is correct aggregation, not a worse metric.

options.text: Percentiles can't be averaged; you must merge the underlying histograms and compute p99 from the combined distribution
options.explanation: Correct. If one server's requests are all slow, they can make up the whole of the fleet's slowest 1%, so the true fleet p99 is that server's latency, while the average of p99s dilutes it with 19 healthy values. Merge histogram buckets (e.g. Prometheus `histogram_quantile` over summed buckets) instead.

questions.workedExample: Imagine equally loaded servers where one server's requests are all slow. That server can contribute more than the fleet's slowest 1%, even though its p99 is only one of twenty dashboard inputs. Averaging those twenty inputs dilutes the slow server instead of finding the slowest requests. Merge compatible histogram counts, then estimate the percentile from the combined distribution; bucket resolution limits accuracy.

questions.prompt: You're asked to produce a trustworthy p99 latency figure for a service before launch. Which practices help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use scheduled-start latency correction (e.g. `wrk2`), or a suitable open-loop generator that accounts for delayed sends
options.explanation: Correct. Measuring from intended send times includes waiting caused by a stall. wrk2 uses this correction even when actual sending falls behind its planned rate; appropriate open-loop tests can also expose the delayed demand.

options.text: Use a closed-loop tester where each client waits for a response before sending the next request
options.explanation: Incorrect. During a stall a closed-loop client stops sending, so the requests that *would* have suffered the stall are never measured. This is coordinated omission and it flatters the tail.

options.text: Record latencies into histograms on every host and merge the histograms before computing p99
options.explanation: Correct. Percentiles must come from the combined distribution. Merged histograms estimate the fleet-wide p99 from the combined distribution; accuracy depends on bucket resolution.

options.text: Report the average of each host's p99
options.explanation: Incorrect. Percentiles can't be averaged; one degraded host can be hidden almost completely.

options.text: Also measure from the client side, not only inside the server's request handler
options.explanation: Correct. Handler timing misses network time, TLS, load balancer hops and time spent queued before the handler starts, which is often where the tail lives.

questions.workedExample:
Consider a 1-second server stall during a test at 1,000 req/s.

```
planned rate: ~1,000 starts during stall
corrected: delay includes intended start
closed loop (10 clients):
            ~10 requests delayed,
            senders paused, rest unseen
```

The closed-loop test records about 100x fewer slow requests, so its p99 looks far better than what real users, who don't politely wait, would see. Use a tester that accounts for intended arrival times, merge histograms with suitable bucket resolution, and measure from the client.

lessons.title: Control the tail amplified by fan-out
lessons.summary: Explain why more parallel backends increase exposure to slow responses, and choose remedies for variability.
lessons.body:
The previous unit introduced p99 and p99.9: thresholds near the slow end of a latency distribution. In a service that waits for many parallel backend calls, those rare slow responses can become the normal user experience.

## Why the tail matters more than you'd think

**Your heaviest users hit the tail most.** A user loading a page that makes 50 backend calls is much more likely to experience at least one slow call. Amazon's Dynamo paper describes service-level targets set at p99.9 rather than the mean or median, so that *every* customer gets a good experience, including those with the longest histories and so the most expensive requests.

**Fan-out amplifies the tail.** If a request fans out to several servers in parallel and must wait for all of them, it's as slow as the slowest. With independent 1%-slow backends, one call is rarely slow, but about 63% of requests waiting for 100 calls encounter at least one slow response. More calls create more opportunities for delay.

The reference relationship is useful when estimating that exposure:

```formula reference
P_slow = 1 − (1 − q)^n
where
P_slow: the probability that a user request is slow, i.e. at least one of its backend calls is slow, from 0 to 1
q: the probability that any one server exceeds the chosen slow-response threshold; here 0.01 (1%)
n: the number of servers the request fans out to in parallel
^: "to the power of": 0.99^10 means 10 copies of 0.99 multiplied together
In words: when a request needs every backend, more independent backend calls make it more likely to encounter at least one slow response.
```

The formula assumes each server is slow independently of the others. Correlated slowness (a shared overloaded database, say) changes the numbers.

At 100-way fan-out, most requests (63%) wait for at least one server's p99-or-worse response, so a single server's tail becomes your typical latency. This is the central point of Dean and Barroso's paper *The Tail at Scale*. Mitigations include **hedged requests** (send a second copy after the p95 time elapses and use whichever returns first), tied requests, and reducing variability at the source. Tied requests let a replica cancel its queued duplicate when another replica starts the work. Isolating or scheduling background work reduces interference; returning partial results after a deadline can cap latency when the application permits missing results.

## Key takeaways
- A request waiting for every shard inherits the slowest response.
- Independent 1%-slow shards make about 63% of 100-way requests slow; shared causes change that model.
- Hedging, partial results and reducing background-work interference address tail variability, with their own costs.

## Further reading
- [The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf)
- [Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

questions.prompt: A search service waits for all 50 shard replies. Each shard occasionally pauses independently. If the fan-out grows while each shard's pause behaviour stays unchanged, what happens to user-visible slow responses?

options.text: They stay at the per-shard rate
options.explanation: Incorrect. The request can be delayed by any shard, so the user experiences more opportunities for a pause.

options.text: They become more common because there are more chances to encounter a slow shard
options.explanation: Correct. Waiting for every reply makes the slowest shard determine completion time.

options.text: They become less common because parallel calls average away pauses
options.explanation: Incorrect. The service waits for the slowest result; it does not complete at the average shard time.

options.text: They occur only when every shard pauses together
options.explanation: Incorrect. One slow shard is enough to delay a request that needs all replies.

questions.workedExample: Follow one request: all fast replies still cannot complete it while one required shard is paused. Adding independently variable calls creates more chances for that event. Correlated causes change the numerical model; reducing variability, safely hedging or permitting partial results can address the user-visible tail.

questions.prompt: A service's p95 latency is 40 ms and p99.9 is 900 ms, mostly due to occasional GC pauses on random replicas. You add **hedged requests**: if no response arrives within 40 ms, send a duplicate to another replica and take the first reply. Assume pauses are independent and there is capacity for the duplicates. What is the main effect and request-count cost?

options.text: Tail latency gets worse because of the extra load
options.explanation: Incorrect under the stated spare-capacity assumption. Racing an independent replica can reduce the tail; near saturation, duplicated work could instead worsen it.

options.text: Median latency halves, for 100% extra load
options.explanation: Incorrect. Duplicating every request would double load; hedging only after the p95 time leaves the median unaffected because most requests finish before the hedge fires.

options.text: Tail latency can drop sharply, for roughly 5% more requests
options.explanation: Correct. Roughly the slowest 5% pass the p95 threshold and trigger another request. That is a request-count increase, not a promise of only 5% more CPU or I/O: resource cost depends on duplicate work and cancellation.

options.text: No effect, because GC pauses affect all replicas simultaneously
options.explanation: Incorrect. The scenario says pauses hit *random* replicas, i.e. they're independent. Hedging works precisely because a second replica is unlikely to be paused at the same moment.

questions.workedExample: Most requests finish before the p95 deadline and receive no duplicate. A slower request races a second replica after 40 ms; independent pauses make that replica less likely to share the same delay. This can substantially reduce tail latency when spare capacity exists. Roughly 5% more requests does not mean exactly 5% more resource use. Only duplicate operations safely, cancel the loser where possible, and measure the added work and resulting tail. Tied requests let a replica cancel its queued duplicate when another replica starts work.

questions.prompt: A search service fans out to 100 shards and its p99 is dominated by occasional slow shards. Traces confirm independent per-replica pauses dominate the tail, with no saturated CPU, I/O or worker-pool bottleneck; average CPU utilisation is about 25%. Which changes are likely to **reduce p99**? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hedge requests to a replica shard after the p95 time has elapsed
options.explanation: Correct. Independent slow shards are exactly the case hedging fixes, for a few percent additional requests in the cited experiment; resource overhead depends on cancellation and the duplicated work.

options.text: Return partial results after a deadline if a few shards haven't replied
options.explanation: Correct. When the product permits missing results, a deadline can cap waiting instead of requiring every shard's reply.

options.text: Run compaction and other background work on a schedule or on isolated cores
options.explanation: Correct. Background work is a common source of variability. Reducing variance at the source is one of Dean and Barroso's main recommendations.

options.text: Double the number of servers per shard while keeping fan-out the same
options.explanation: Incorrect. The stated traces rule out saturation as the main cause here; 25% average CPU alone would not prove that. More capacity won't stop individual servers having pauses, so the fan-out maths is unchanged.

options.text: Raise the client timeout from 1 s to 5 s
options.explanation: Incorrect. A longer timeout does not shorten any backend pause. It permits longer waiting before giving up and may change which requests are included in reported latency.

questions.workedExample: The traces identify independent replica pauses rather than saturation. A hedge can race a paused replica, and isolating background work can reduce pauses at their source. A deadline with partial results stops waiting for every shard if missing data is acceptable. More idle capacity alone does not remove the stated pause mechanism. Hedged operations must be safe to duplicate, and the added work must fit available capacity.

lessons.title: Compare latency orders of magnitude carefully
lessons.summary: Use hypothetical timings to spot important differences, then measure the actual workload before designing around them.
lessons.body:
A useful estimate distinguishes nanoseconds, microseconds and milliseconds. Otherwise a small-looking number can hide a much slower operation. A microsecond is a thousand nanoseconds; a millisecond is a thousand microseconds.

## Use a timing table as a hypothesis

The following values are **hypothetical exercise inputs**, not current hardware benchmarks:

| Operation | Assumed time |
|---|---|
| L1 cache reference | 1 ns |
| Main memory reference | 100 ns |
| Random SSD read | 100 µs |
| Same-datacentre round trip | 0.5 ms |
| HDD seek | 10 ms |
| Distant-region round trip | 70 ms |

Converting to a common unit shows that these operations can occupy very different scales. Under these assumptions, memory access is much cheaper than a random storage read, and a distant round trip costs far more than either. The useful conclusion is where to investigate, rather than a ratio to memorise.

> [!note] Content gap: reproducible measurements
> These assumed values do not come from one measured hardware and workload configuration. Do not use them as capacity promises. Measure payload size, access pattern, caching, concurrency and load on the intended system.

A request can pay an expensive operation many times. Several sequential distant calls may dominate its latency even when each carries few bytes. Batching, overlapping independent work or moving computation near the data can avoid those repeated waits.

## Access pattern matters

A storage device does not have one latency for every operation. A mechanical disk may need to move its head before a random read, whereas sequential access can stream nearby data. SSD behaviour also depends on size, load and device details. A network cache adds a network exchange even when its own data is in RAM.

Use the table to ask specific questions: is this request waiting on many random reads, a distant dependency, or a saturated resource? Validate the answer with timings and traces.

## Throughput can be high while latency is poor

Moving a large batch efficiently does not guarantee a fast first result. A bulk physical transfer can deliver a huge quantity per trip while taking hours to deliver any of it. That same distinction applies when buffering or batching network and storage work.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a lorry carrying drives
> A lorry can carry many drives in one journey, but the recipient waits for the journey to finish.
>
> **How it maps:** Total data delivered per journey can imply high average throughput, while the time until delivery remains long. Bandwidth and latency answer different questions.
>
> **Where it stops:** Physical transfers have loading, handling and copying costs. They are useful only for suitable bulk jobs, not interactive requests.

## Key takeaways
- Compare durations in consistent units before deciding which cost matters.
- Illustrative timing tables suggest hypotheses; measure the actual workload and access pattern.
- Repeated sequential exchanges can dominate latency even with small payloads.
- High bulk throughput does not imply a quick first response.

## Further reading
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
- [The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf)

questions.prompt: A team compares in-memory access, a local SSD read and a distant network round trip using an illustrative timing table. Which conclusions are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Convert all durations to a common unit before comparing them
options.explanation: Correct. Nanoseconds, microseconds and milliseconds differ greatly, so mismatched units can reverse the apparent scale.

options.text: Use the table to form a hypothesis, then measure the actual hardware and workload
options.explanation: Correct. Illustrative times explain possible orders of magnitude without being current capacity guarantees.

options.text: Treat every operation labelled SSD as having the same latency
options.explanation: Incorrect. Access pattern, size, hardware, load and caching all affect a storage measurement.

options.text: Reducing sequential distant exchanges can help even when their payloads are tiny
options.explanation: Correct. A small payload does not remove the wait for a reply across a long distance.

options.text: A bandwidth upgrade removes propagation delay
options.explanation: Incorrect. Faster transmission does not remove the time a signal needs to travel.

questions.workedExample: First compare like units, then ask which work is on the critical path. A large difference suggests where to investigate, but the table cannot certify today's latency for a different deployment. For a chatty distant protocol, repeated waits can dominate even when transmitting the bytes is cheap.
