lessons.title: Translate availability targets into error budgets
lessons.summary: Distinguish availability, reliability and durability, and turn nines into measurable SLO budgets.
lessons.body:
"Is the system up?" sounds like a yes/no question. In practice, availability is a number you design for, measure and trade against cost. This lesson explains how the target becomes a practical failure allowance.

## Availability vs reliability vs durability

These words are often used interchangeably. They shouldn't be.

- **Availability**: the fraction of time (or of requests) the system is able to serve correctly. "99.9% of minutes this month the API returned successful responses."
- **Reliability**: the probability the system works correctly *without failure* over a period. A system that fails for 100 ms every minute is about 99.83% available but terrible for reliability: almost any long-running job or long-lived connection will hit a failure.
- **Durability**: the probability that stored data is *not lost*. Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability but offers a much lower availability SLA. Data can be safe yet temporarily unreachable.

There are two common ways to turn availability into a number: count time, or count requests.

Availability can count **successful time** or **successful requests**. Choose what counts as good service and the observation window before comparing targets.

For a 30-day month, 99.9% time-based availability allows about 43 minutes of downtime. A request-based 99.9% target allows one failed request per thousand. These allowances differ when traffic varies or an incident affects only some requests.

> [!note] Time-based vs request-based
> Request-based availability is usually more meaningful for large services (Google SRE favours it), because a 5-minute outage at 3 a.m. affects far fewer users than one at peak.

## The nines

Availability is usually quoted in "nines". Here's the equivalent downtime, using a 365.25-day year and an average month (year/12):

| Availability | Downtime/year | Downtime/month |
|---|---|---|
| 99% (two nines) | 3.65 days | 7.3 hours |
| 99.9% | 8.77 hours | 43.8 min |
| 99.95% | 4.38 hours | 21.9 min |
| 99.99% | 52.6 min | 4.4 min |
| 99.999% | 5.26 min | 26 s |

The formula behind the table: the fraction of time you are allowed to be down is 1 minus the availability.

```formula reference
D = (1 − A) × T
where
D: the allowed downtime in the period, in minutes
A: the time-based availability target as a fraction, such as 0.999 for 99.9%
T: the length of the observation period, in minutes
In words: the share of time outside the availability target determines the downtime allowance. A stricter target leaves less room for outages in the same period.
```

Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10x. The cost of achieving it depends on the architecture and failure modes; there is no universal cost multiplier. At 99.999%, you have 26 seconds a month. Manual detection and recovery can easily consume that budget, so automated recovery is usually essential.

> [!tip] Think in error budgets
> If your SLO is 99.9%, you have a 0.1% **error budget**: about 43 minutes a month. Spend it on deploys, experiments and incidents. When it's gone, slow down releases. This turns availability into an engineering trade-off rather than a moral absolute.

## SLIs, SLOs and SLAs (briefly)

- **SLI** (indicator): the measurement, e.g. proportion of requests returning non-5xx in under 300 ms.
- **SLO** (objective): the target for that SLI, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days.
- **SLA** (agreement): a contract with consequences, e.g. service credits. AWS's EC2 Region-Level SLA specifies 99.99% under its stated multi-AZ deployment and measurement conditions; an individual instance has a separate commitment.

SLAs are normally looser than internal SLOs, so you're warned before you owe customers money. The reliability and observability module goes deeper.

## Key takeaways
- Availability measures successful service, reliability measures failure-free operation, and durability measures retained data.
- Time-based and request-based availability weight partial and peak-hour outages differently.
- An SLI is a measurement, an SLO its target, and an SLA a contractual commitment; the remaining failure allowance is the error budget.

## Further reading
- [Availability table (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/availability-table/)
- [Embracing Risk (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)
- [Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

questions.prompt: A service raises its time-based availability target from 99.9% to 99.99% over the same monthly window. What changes operationally?

options.text: The allowed downtime grows because the percentage is larger
options.explanation: Incorrect. A higher successful-time target leaves less time for unavailability.

options.text: The downtime allowance becomes ten times smaller, making detection and recovery speed more important
options.explanation: Correct. The unavailable share falls from one part in a thousand to one part in ten thousand.

options.text: No operational change is needed if the target is only documentation
options.explanation: Incorrect. A target should drive measured behaviour and recovery planning; relabelling does not improve the service.

options.text: The target proves stored data can never be lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability concerns successful service; data-loss risk is durability.

questions.workedExample: Keep the measurement window fixed and compare the remaining failure allowance. An extra nine removes most of the old downtime budget, so a manual response that fit the previous target may consume the new one. Check detection, failover and recovery against that smaller allowance.

questions.prompt: An object store advertises 99.999999999% durability and a hypothetical time-based 99.9% monthly availability commitment. A product manager asks: "So we'll basically never be unable to read a file?" What's the accurate answer?

options.text: Yes; eleven nines means effectively always readable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is about data not being *lost*; it says nothing about whether you can reach the data at a given moment.

options.text: Yes, as long as you enable versioning
options.explanation: Incorrect. Versioning protects against accidental overwrites and deletes, not against the service being unreachable.

options.text: No; eleven nines durability means about 1 in 10¹¹ reads will fail
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is measured per object per year (probability of loss), not per read. Failed reads are an availability matter.

options.text: No; durability describes loss risk, while this time-based availability target allows roughly 43 minutes of unavailability in a 30-day month
options.explanation: Correct. The object can be safely stored on many disks yet temporarily unreachable due to network, control-plane or regional problems. The 99.9% SLA is the relevant number for 'can I read it right now?'

questions.workedExample: Ask two separate questions: will the object still exist, and can the service return it now? Durability concerns the first; availability concerns the second. A safely stored object can remain unreachable during a network or service outage. The hypothetical 99.9% time-based monthly commitment allows some unavailable time; its measurement and exclusions determine what counts. If access is critical, evaluate caching, delivery paths and regional failure recovery rather than relying on the durability figure.

questions.prompt: Two incidents last equally long. One fails a small share of requests overnight; the other fails most requests at peak traffic. Under a request-based SLO, how should their error-budget impact be compared?

options.text: Count degraded minutes only; their impact is equal
options.explanation: Incorrect. That ignores both traffic volume and the share of requests that failed.

options.text: Count failed requests relative to the allowance for the SLO window
options.explanation: Correct. A request-based budget weights the failures actually experienced by requests, so the peak incident can consume much more.

options.text: Use only the largest failure percentage reached during either incident
options.explanation: Incorrect. Duration and request volume also determine how many requests failed.

options.text: Ignore partial failures unless every request fails
options.explanation: Incorrect. Partial outages still produce bad requests that consume the budget.

questions.workedExample: Identify the SLI's unit before measuring impact. A request-based availability SLI counts good and bad requests across the chosen window. The same number of incident minutes can contain very different numbers of bad requests. Use the actual counts and apply the agreed budget policy.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets are **true**? Select all that apply.

options.text: An SLA is normally set looser than the internal SLO for the same service
options.explanation: Correct. The gap means you breach your own objective, and react, before you owe customers credits.

options.text: When the error budget is exhausted, a common policy is to pause risky releases and focus on reliability
options.explanation: Correct. This is the core of an error-budget policy: the budget turns the speed-versus-stability argument into an agreed rule.

options.text: A 100% availability SLO is the ideal target for any user-facing service
options.explanation: Incorrect. 100% is unachievable, users can't tell the difference beyond their own network's reliability, and it leaves no budget for change. Google SRE explicitly argues against it.

options.text: The SLI is the contractual penalty paid when targets are missed
options.explanation: Incorrect. The SLI is the measurement itself (e.g. share of requests succeeding under 300 ms). Penalties belong to the SLA.

options.text: With request-based availability, an outage at peak hour consumes more budget than the same-length outage overnight
options.explanation: Correct. More requests fail at peak, so more of the budget is spent, which matches the real user impact.

questions.workedExample: An SLI measures service behaviour, an SLO sets the desired level, and an SLA records a contractual commitment and consequences. The error budget is the allowed share of bad service outside the SLO. A request-based budget is consumed by failed requests, so an otherwise identical peak-hour outage spends more than an overnight one. Teams can agree to pause risky changes when the budget is exhausted; that is a policy based on user impact.

lessons.title: Model redundancy with capacity and shared failures
lessons.summary: Explain how redundancy depends on independent failures, working failover and enough survivor capacity.
lessons.body:
Redundancy helps when another component can take over. Model that benefit using the survivors the workload actually needs, then account for failures that can affect every copy together.

## Components in parallel

If the system works as long as **at least one** of several redundant components works, they're in **parallel**. The system fails only if *all* fail, so work out the chance that every one is down and subtract it from 1:

```formula reference
A_total = 1 − (1 − A_1)(1 − A_2)
where
A_total: availability of a pair when either member alone can carry the load, as a fraction from 0 to 1
A_1, A_2: availability of the first and second member, each as a fraction from 0 to 1
In words: either member can keep the service running, so the pair is unavailable only when both are down. This estimate assumes independent failures and immediate, successful failover.
```

```
            +--> [App 99%] --+
client ->LB-|                |-> ok
            +--> [App 99%] --+
```

For two independent 99%-available servers, with immediate switching and either able to carry the load, the model gives 99.99% availability. A third reduces the chance of all being down further. The gain depends on those assumptions.

> [!warning] Redundancy needs spare capacity
> The parallel formula assumes **one survivor can carry the whole load**. If peak traffic needs both servers, losing either one at peak overloads the other, and the pair behaves like two components in series. Plan for **N+1** (or N+2): enough servers that the system still meets its load with one, or one zone, gone.

When some number of identical servers are needed out of a larger group (written "k of n"), the system is up while at least that many are up. For three 99% servers where any two can carry peak load, add up the chances of the states that work: all three up, or exactly two up.

For three independent 99%-available servers where any two can carry the load, the model gives about 99.97% availability. This is lower than the any-one-of-three case because states with only one survivor now count as failures.

The useful question is which survivor combinations can actually serve peak traffic, rather than how many copies exist.

## The big caveat: independence

The formulas above assume failures are **independent**. In reality, they often aren't:

- Two servers in the same rack share a power supply and switch.
- Replicas running the same software share the same bugs (a bad deploy or a leap-second bug takes them all out at once).
- A bad config push hits every region.
- Failover itself can fail, or take minutes. The parallel formula assumes switching is instant; a 5-minute failover that happens four times a year is 20 minutes of downtime the formula never shows.

Two 99% servers on the same host don't give you 99.99%. This is why cloud providers offer **availability zones** (separate power, cooling and networking) and why multi-region designs exist. It's also why staged rollouts matter: they stop a single bad change from becoming a correlated failure.

> [!warning] Redundancy you haven't tested is a hope, not a design
> A standby database that has never been failed over to is likely to surprise you. Practise failovers regularly (game days, chaos engineering).

## Key takeaways
- Parallel availability improves only when surviving components can serve the required load.
- Two-of-three capacity has different availability from any-one-of-three capacity.
- Shared power, software, config and slow failover invalidate the simplest independent, instant-switch model.

## Further reading
- [Availability and Beyond (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience.html)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: Three redundant app servers fail independently, either one can carry the full load, and failover is immediate and reliable. Ignoring the load balancer, when is the tier unavailable?

options.text: Whenever any one server is down
options.explanation: Incorrect. The remaining servers can still serve the full workload.

options.text: Whenever fewer than all three are up
options.explanation: Incorrect. This treats redundant alternatives as required serial components.

options.text: Never, because three copies guarantee availability
options.explanation: Incorrect. Independent failures can still overlap, and real systems can also have common failures.

options.text: Only while all three are down together
options.explanation: Correct. Under the stated capacity and failover assumptions, any survivor keeps the tier available.

questions.workedExample: Start with the success condition: one surviving server is enough. A single failure or two simultaneous failures therefore do not stop the tier. All three being down is the failure state in this simplified model. Shared power, configuration bugs or slow failover invalidate its assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which of these are likely to make real-world availability **lower** than the parallel-redundancy formula predicts? Select all that apply.

options.text: All replicas run in the same rack on the same top-of-rack switch
options.explanation: Correct. A switch or power failure takes out all replicas together: a correlated failure the formula (which assumes independence) doesn't model.

options.text: A config change is pushed to all replicas simultaneously
options.explanation: Correct. A bad config is a common-mode failure that breaks every replica at once, so redundancy provides no protection. Staged rollouts mitigate this.

options.text: Failover takes 3 minutes to detect a failure and promote a standby
options.explanation: Correct. The formula assumes switching is instant. Three minutes of failover per incident is real downtime.

options.text: Replicas are spread across three availability zones
options.explanation: Incorrect. This *reduces* correlation by putting replicas in separate failure domains, bringing reality closer to the formula's prediction.

options.text: All replicas share an identical software bug triggered by a specific date
options.explanation: Correct. Identical software fails identically. Leap-second and date-rollover bugs have taken down whole fleets at once.

questions.workedExample: Check the assumptions behind the redundancy model: independent failures, enough survivor capacity, and immediate successful switching. A shared rack, global bad configuration or shared bug can affect all copies together. Slow promotion adds downtime even when a healthy standby exists. Separate zones reduce some shared infrastructure risks, while staged changes and tested failovers address others. Do not count a common-cause failure twice if it is already included in measured availability.

questions.prompt: A three-server tier can handle peak traffic with any two servers, but one alone cannot. Which statement should guide its redundancy model?

options.text: Use an any-one-survivor model because there are three copies
options.explanation: Incorrect. One copy cannot meet peak demand, so that model counts overloaded states as available.

options.text: Require all three servers to be healthy
options.explanation: Incorrect. The stated capacity allows one failure without losing service.

options.text: Count the tier as available when at least two servers are healthy
options.explanation: Correct. The success states must reflect survivor capacity at the required load.

options.text: Ignore capacity and model only whether a process is running
options.explanation: Incorrect. A running process that cannot serve the load does not satisfy the service requirement.

questions.workedExample: Test the survivor combinations against peak load. Three up works, and any two up works. One up does not. The availability model must count exactly those working combinations, then account for shared failures and switching delays.

questions.prompt: An active-passive service has a healthy, fully sized standby in another region. Every primary failure still causes a 15-minute outage while the team detects it and promotes the standby. Why does an instant-failover redundancy model overstate availability?

options.text: Two regions must always be modelled as required components in series
options.explanation: Incorrect. Either region can serve; they are alternatives, although switching between them costs time.

options.text: It omits the downtime spent detecting and completing each failover
options.explanation: Correct. A healthy standby does not serve users until the failover process makes it usable.

options.text: The standby's capacity is irrelevant to availability
options.explanation: Incorrect. Failover cannot restore the service if the standby lacks capacity.

options.text: Independent region failures make promotion time disappear
options.explanation: Incorrect. Independence concerns overlapping failures, not the delay in switching to a survivor.

questions.workedExample: Trace the outage from the user's view. The standby remains healthy, but users wait while failure is detected, a decision is made, promotion completes and traffic moves. That is real downtime outside an instant-switch model. Measure and rehearse the whole recovery path; automation must be safe as well as fast.

lessons.title: Find availability risks along a request path
lessons.summary: Identify required dependencies, distinguish redundant alternatives, and move optional work off the critical path.
lessons.body:
The previous unit modelled redundant components in parallel. A real request usually also needs several different tiers to work together, so its availability combines both kinds of relationship.

## Components in series

If a request needs **every** component to work, the components are in **series**. Assuming independent failures, the chance that all of them are up at once is the product of their availabilities:

```formula reference
A_total = A_1 × A_2 × … × A_n
where
A_total: the availability of the whole chain, as a fraction from 0 to 1
A_1, A_2, A_n: the availability of the first, second and last (n-th) component, each as a fraction (99.9% = 0.999)
n: the number of components the request needs
…: and so on: one factor for every component in between
In words: the chain works only when every required link works. With independent failures, multiplying their availabilities estimates how often they all work together.
```

```
client -> [LB] -> [App] -> [DB]
         99.99%  99.9%   99.95%
```

In this example, all three tiers must be healthy. Their independent modelled availability is about 99.84%, below each individual tier.

A required dependency creates another way for the request to fail. The chain cannot be more available than its least available required tier; with independent imperfect tiers it is less available. Adding synchronous dependencies therefore consumes the request path's reliability budget.

This is the mathematical reason to:

- Remove dependencies from the critical path (do work asynchronously).
- Degrade gracefully: show the page without recommendations rather than failing it.
- Be suspicious of deep synchronous microservice call chains.

## Combining them

Real systems mix both. Compute parallel groups first, then multiply the groups in series:

First identify the redundant alternatives inside each tier. Check that survivors have capacity and that failover works. Then treat the tiers the request still needs as a chain. Redundant app servers do not remove the database as a required dependency, and a shared failure can still affect several tiers together.

## Key takeaways
- A request needing every independent dependency has availability equal to the product of their availabilities.
- Calculate each parallel group first, then multiply required groups in series.
- Asynchronous work and graceful degradation reduce the dependencies that must succeed for the core request.

## Further reading
- [Availability and Beyond (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience.html)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: A request must pass through a load balancer, app tier and database. Each can fail independently. How does the request path's availability compare with the individual tiers?

options.text: It is lower than every required tier's availability when each has a nonzero failure risk
options.explanation: Correct. The request fails whenever any required tier is unavailable, creating more failure opportunities than one tier alone.

options.text: It equals the least available tier automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. That tier sets an upper bound, but the other required tiers also fail.

options.text: It equals the most available tier
options.explanation: Incorrect. A healthy load balancer cannot complete a request while the required database is down.

options.text: It improves simply because there are more components
options.explanation: Incorrect. These components are required stages, rather than redundant alternatives.

questions.workedExample: Trace one failure at a time. A failed app tier blocks the request even if the database is healthy; a failed database also blocks it. Independent required dependencies therefore lower whole-path availability. Removing optional blocking work or adding valid redundancy changes those success conditions.

questions.prompt: Checkout must meet a strict availability target but synchronously requires six downstream services, including optional recommendations. Its own tier already only just meets the target. What is the best approach?

options.text: Take non-essential dependencies off the critical path (async or graceful degradation) and add redundancy to the essential ones
options.explanation: Correct. Reducing the number of things that must *all* work raises the series ceiling. E.g. recommendations and loyalty points can fail gracefully; inventory and payment remain required and get redundancy or retries to a second provider.

options.text: Ask every dependency to raise its availability to 99.95%
options.explanation: Incorrect on its own. Several required components each meeting the whole-path target still add failure opportunities; the checkout tier also needs margin.

options.text: It's fine: the weakest dependency is 99.9%, close to the target
options.explanation: Incorrect. A request needs every synchronous dependency to succeed. Their additional failures cannot be ignored because each individual figure looks close to the target.

options.text: Add retries to every call; this makes each dependency 100% available
options.explanation: Incorrect. Retries help with transient errors but not with a dependency that's down for minutes, and aggressive retries can amplify an outage (retry storms).

questions.workedExample: Classify each dependency by whether checkout must fail without it. Recommendations can often be omitted; inventory and payment still need an authoritative safe path. Move optional work off the blocking path, improve essential dependencies and recovery, and give checkout itself reliability margin. Retries need limits and safe semantics, and more replicas do not remove common software or configuration failures.

lessons.title: Improve availability by shortening recovery
lessons.summary: Use MTBF and MTTR to identify investments in detection, diagnosis, failover and verification.
lessons.body:
Redundancy is only part of resilience. When service does fail, reducing the time users wait for recovery can be a more practical investment than trying to eliminate every failure.

## MTBF and MTTR

Two quantities define steady-state availability:

- **MTBF** (mean time between failures): how long, on average, the system runs before failing.
- **MTTR** (mean time to repair/recovery): how long, on average, it takes to restore service.

Over a long run, the system cycles between working (for MTBF on average) and being repaired (for MTTR on average). The fraction of each cycle spent working is the availability:

```formula reference
A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)
where
A: the steady-state availability, the long-run fraction of time the system is up
MTBF: mean time between failures, the average time it runs before failing, in hours (h)
MTTR: mean time to repair (or recovery), the average time to restore service after a failure, in the same unit as MTBF
h: hour
In words: availability is the up-time of a typical cycle divided by the whole cycle, up-time plus repair time.
```

The model assumes repeated working and recovery cycles at stable average rates. It describes long-run availability, not the duration or impact of a particular incident.

There are two levers:

1. **Increase MTBF**: better hardware, fewer risky changes, more testing.
2. **Decrease MTTR**: faster detection, automated failover, quick rollbacks, good runbooks.

Lowering MTTR is often cheaper and more effective. Cutting MTTR from 60 minutes to 6 gives the same availability gain as making failures 10x rarer. Recovery includes **detection**, **diagnosis**, **repair or failover**, and **verification**. Measuring those stages reveals where the delay actually occurs; faster repairs cannot help much if nobody notices the failure for an hour.

Each piece suggests an investment: alerting on symptoms (detect), good dashboards and tracing (diagnose), automated failover and one-click rollback (fix).

Related terms you'll see: **MTTF** (mean time *to* failure, for non-repairable parts) and **MTTD** (mean time to detect).

## Key takeaways
- Long-run availability depends on time working relative to time working plus recovery time.
- Making recovery ten times faster has the same modelled availability effect as making failures ten times rarer.
- Separate detection, diagnosis, repair and verification to choose concrete recovery improvements.

## Further reading
- [Availability and Beyond (AWS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience.html)
- [Embracing Risk (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)

questions.prompt: A database fails just as often after a change, but automated failover restores service much faster. What should improve, assuming the failover works safely?

options.text: Nothing, because failure frequency alone determines availability
options.explanation: Incorrect. Availability also depends on how long service remains unavailable after a failure.

options.text: Durability automatically becomes perfect
options.explanation: Incorrect. Faster restoration does not prove that acknowledged data survives every failure.

options.text: Availability improves because each failure consumes less unavailable time
options.explanation: Correct. Shorter recovery increases the share of time service is usable even with unchanged failure frequency.

options.text: The mean time between failures must fall
options.explanation: Incorrect. The change concerns recovery time; the scenario keeps failure frequency unchanged.

questions.workedExample: Separate frequency from duration. The same number of failures can cause much less total downtime when detection and recovery are faster. Check that the automated path preserves correctness, and include detection and verification when measuring recovery.

questions.prompt: Which investments mainly reduce **MTTR** (mean time to recovery)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Alerting on user-facing symptoms such as error rate and latency
options.explanation: Correct. You can't start fixing what you haven't noticed. Symptom alerts shrink time to detect.

options.text: One-click or automatic rollback of deploys
options.explanation: Correct. For an incident caused by a change, reverting quickly can shrink time to fix.

options.text: Distributed tracing and good dashboards
options.explanation: Correct. They shrink time to diagnose by showing which component is failing and why.

options.text: Buying hardware with a longer rated lifetime
options.explanation: Incorrect. This raises MTBF (failures happen less often). It does nothing to speed up recovery when a failure does happen.

options.text: Adding a code-review step before every change
options.explanation: Incorrect. Review aims to prevent failures, so it targets MTBF. It doesn't make recovery faster.

questions.workedExample:
Split MTTR into its parts and map each option:

| Option | Shrinks |
|---|---|
| Symptom alerts | Detect |
| Fast rollback | Fix |
| Tracing, dashboards | Diagnose |
| Longer-lived hardware | (MTBF) |
| Code review | (MTBF) |

Both levers matter, but for a fixed MTBF, downtime per incident is proportional to MTTR; halving recovery time approximately halves long-run unavailability when MTTR is small relative to MTBF.

lessons.title: Choose scaling strategies and expose hidden state
lessons.summary: Compare scale-up with scale-out, and identify the state that prevents an app instance being safely replaced.
lessons.body:
A system is **scalable** if it can handle more load by adding resources, while keeping performance acceptable and cost roughly proportional to load.

"Load" can mean many things: requests per second, number of users, data volume, write rate or number of concurrent connections. Always ask "scalable along *which* dimension?". A system that handles 10x more reads may not handle 10x more writes.

## Vertical scaling (scale up)

Make the machine bigger: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks.

**Pros**

- Usually no application changes. A bigger Postgres instance remains one Postgres instance, although configuration and resource limits may need adjustment.
- No distributed-systems problems: no network partitions between nodes, no consistency puzzles.
- Surprisingly far-reaching. Cloud instances with hundreds of vCPUs and multiple terabytes of RAM are readily available.

**Cons**

- **A ceiling.** Eventually there's no bigger machine.
- **Cost at the top end.** On your own hardware, the biggest servers cost disproportionately more per unit of capacity. Cloud prices vary by instance family, region and purchase model. A continuously running fixed-size instance must be paid for even during quiet periods; compare current prices rather than assuming a universal cost curve.
- **A single point of failure.** One big machine is still one machine.
- **Downtime to resize**, in many setups.

> [!tip] Don't dismiss scaling up
> Stack Overflow famously served huge traffic from a handful of powerful SQL Server machines for years. Scaling up is often the cheapest, simplest first move, especially for databases. A common path is: scale the database up, add read replicas and a cache for reads, and shard only when *writes* outgrow the biggest sensible machine.

## Horizontal scaling (scale out)

Add more machines and spread the load across them.

**Pros**

- Near-unlimited capacity, if the workload partitions well.
- Redundancy comes naturally: losing one of 20 nodes loses 5% of capacity.
- Commodity hardware and elastic autoscaling.

**Cons**

- Requires load balancing, service discovery and distributed coordination.
- Data must be partitioned or replicated, which brings consistency trade-offs.
- More moving parts to operate and debug.

```
 vertical             horizontal

 +--------+       +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+
 |        |       |  | |  | |  | |  |
 |  BIG   |       +--+ +--+ +--+ +--+
 |        |            ^
 +--------+       load balancer
```

## Stateless vs stateful

The single most important property for horizontal scaling is whether a component is **stateless**.

A **stateless** service keeps no client-specific data between requests. Any instance can handle any request. Session data, uploaded files and caches live in shared external stores (a database, Redis, S3).

```
          +--> [app 1] --+
client -> LB-> [app 2] ---> Redis / DB
          +--> [app 3] --+
```

Why stateless services are easy to scale:

- Add or remove instances freely; the load balancer needs no stickiness.
- An instance crash loses nothing except in-flight requests.
- Autoscaling, rolling deploys and spot instances become easier, but still require graceful shutdown, retry-safe requests and sufficient capacity in backing services.

This is the "processes" factor of the Twelve-Factor App: processes are stateless and share nothing; state lives in backing services.

A **stateful** component holds data that matters: databases, caches, message brokers, WebSocket connection servers, game servers. Scaling them needs answers to:

- **Where does each piece of data live?** (partitioning, or sharding)
- **How are copies kept in sync?** (replication)
- **What happens when a node joins, leaves or dies?** (rebalancing, failover)

These are the hard problems covered in the databases, consistency and messaging modules. A common architecture pattern is to **push state down** into a few well-understood stateful systems (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, S3) and keep everything above them stateless.

> [!warning] Hidden state
> In-memory authoritative sessions, unpersisted local uploads and uncoordinated rate-limit counters create hidden correctness-critical state. Disposable local caches can be compatible with a stateless service when correctness does not depend on their contents. Symptoms: users logged out randomly, rate limits that are 10x too lenient with 10 instances.

## Key takeaways
- Name the load dimension you need to scale: reads, writes, data or connections.
- Scaling up keeps a simpler architecture; scaling out adds coordination and data-placement work.
- Keep correctness-critical state in appropriate backing services; disposable caches differ from authoritative local state.

## Further reading
- [The Twelve-Factor App: Processes](https://12factor.net/processes)
- [Scalability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalability)

questions.prompt: A web app stores logged-in users' sessions in each server's memory. You scale from 1 to 4 servers behind a round-robin load balancer. What happens?

options.text: Users get randomly logged out as requests land on servers that don't hold their session
options.explanation: Correct. A request routed to a different server cannot find a session stored only in the original server's memory. Share authoritative sessions or use an appropriate self-contained token design.

options.text: Everything works; sessions are copied automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing copies in-process memory between servers. Each server only knows the sessions it created itself.

options.text: The app becomes 4× faster for each user
options.explanation: Incorrect. More servers increases total throughput capacity, not single-request speed, and here it introduces a correctness bug.

options.text: The load balancer refuses to start
options.explanation: Incorrect. The load balancer has no idea where sessions are stored; it'll happily distribute requests and expose the bug.

questions.workedExample: The login reaches server 1, which stores the session locally. A later request reaches server 2, which has no copy and treats the user as unauthenticated. More servers do not copy process memory automatically. Put sessions in a shared store or use self-contained signed tokens with an explicit policy for invalidating issued tokens. Sticky routing can hide the issue temporarily, but server failure still loses the session.

questions.prompt: A small team is considering a larger database machine before distributing the data across nodes. Which advantages could justify that first step? Select all that apply.

options.text: No need to partition data or deal with cross-node consistency
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the data on one machine avoids introducing cross-node replication and partitioning into this scaling step.

options.text: Usually requires no application changes
options.explanation: Correct. A larger instance often keeps the same database interface, although configuration, limits and performance still need checking.

options.text: Eliminates single points of failure
options.explanation: Incorrect. The opposite: a single big machine *is* a single point of failure. You still need a replica or standby for availability.

options.text: Cost scales linearly forever
options.explanation: Incorrect. Machines have size limits, and price curves vary by hardware, instance family, region and purchase model.

questions.workedExample: Compare the work introduced by each option. A larger machine can preserve the existing application's data access and avoid new distributed coordination. It still has a hardware ceiling and remains a single point of failure without a separate recovery design. Compare actual prices and measured capacity; neither vertical nor horizontal scaling has a universal cost curve.

questions.prompt: A rate limiter stores a separate per-user counter in each app instance. More instances are added behind a load balancer. Why can users now exceed the intended global limit?

options.text: Each instance automatically receives the other instances' counters
options.explanation: Incorrect. Ordinary process memory is not shared between servers.

options.text: Adding servers divides one global counter automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. There is no shared counter in the stated design.

options.text: Each instance grants its own allowance; coordinate an authoritative limit across instances
options.explanation: Correct. Independent local state permits several allowances for the same user.

options.text: Counters necessarily reset after every request
options.explanation: Incorrect. They can persist locally; the problem is that instances do not coordinate.

questions.workedExample: Trace one user across two instances. Each sees only its own requests and can approve work without knowing what the other has allowed. A shared atomic counter or another coordinated allocation scheme can enforce the intended bound. If using Redis, counter updates and expiry must be atomic, and the service needs an explicit policy when the backing store is unavailable.

questions.prompt: You want app instances that can be killed and replaced at any moment (autoscaling, spot instances). Which designs make an instance **stateful** in a way that breaks this? Select all that apply.

options.text: Uploaded files are written to local disk and processed later by the same instance
options.explanation: Correct. If the instance is terminated, the file is lost. Write uploads to object storage (e.g. S3) instead.

options.text: Pending emails are held in an in-memory queue inside the process
options.explanation: Correct. A crash or scale-in silently drops every queued email. Use a durable external queue.

options.text: Configuration is read from environment variables at startup
options.explanation: Incorrect. Every instance gets the same config from outside, so instances stay interchangeable. This is the Twelve-Factor recommendation.

options.text: Requests carry a signed token that any instance can verify with a shared public key
options.explanation: Incorrect. Self-contained tokens are what let the app tier stay stateless: no instance needs to remember the session.

options.text: Each instance holds long-lived WebSocket connections for its users
options.explanation: Correct. Connections are state: killing the instance drops them, and messages for those users must be routed to whichever instance holds the connection. Such servers need draining and a routing layer.

questions.workedExample:
For each design ask: *if this instance vanished right now, would anything be lost or misrouted?*

| Design | Lost on kill? |
|---|---|
| Local uploads | Files |
| In-memory email queue | Emails |
| Env-var config | Nothing |
| Signed tokens | Nothing |
| WebSockets | Connections |

The fix in each stateful case is to push state down into a dedicated store (object storage, a durable queue) or, for connections, accept a stateful tier and give it graceful draining.

questions.prompt: Your only Postgres server (16 vCPUs) peaks at 70% CPU, mostly from reads. Traffic is expected to double over 18 months. The team is four engineers. What is the most sensible plan?

options.text: Shard the database across 8 nodes now, before it becomes urgent
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sharding adds data-placement and operational complexity. The given read bottleneck should first be measured and compared with simpler read scaling or a larger instance.

options.text: Do nothing; 70% CPU leaves enough headroom for 2x growth
options.explanation: Incorrect. Doubling 70% gives 140%: the server would be saturated well before 18 months, deep into the queueing cliff.

options.text: Rewrite the system as microservices with a database each
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's an organisational and architectural overhaul aimed at a problem a bigger machine and a few replicas solve.

options.text: Scale up to a larger instance and add a cache and read replicas for the read load; plan sharding only if writes outgrow one machine
options.explanation: Correct. Investigate larger-instance capacity and eligible read offload before introducing sharding. Validate the actual workload, freshness requirements and failure behaviour.

questions.workedExample: The existing machine already uses much of its CPU at peak, so doubled traffic needs a capacity plan. The load is mostly reads: benchmark a larger instance, cache repeated eligible reads and use replicas where their freshness contract is acceptable. Measure query and index improvements too. Sharding becomes a candidate if simpler changes cannot meet write, storage or other requirements; the CPU percentage alone does not prove a particular larger machine is enough.

lessons.title: Find the serial and coordination limits of scaling
lessons.summary: Apply Amdahl’s law and node-pair growth to explain why more workers can stop helping or reduce throughput.
lessons.body:
Once a workload can use several workers, the next question is how much speed-up they can provide. Fixed serial work and coordination overhead place different limits on that benefit.

## Amdahl's law: the limit of parallelism

Some part of almost every job can only be done one step at a time (it is **serial**); the rest can be split across workers (it is **parallel**). Gene Amdahl pointed out in 1967 that the serial part limits how much faster extra workers can make the job. Measure the job's time on one worker as 1; the serial share still takes the same time, while the parallel share is divided between the workers:

```formula reference
S(N) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N)
S_max = 1 / (1 − p)
where
S(N): the speed-up with N workers: how many times faster the job runs than on one worker
N: the number of workers (cores, machines) sharing the parallel part
p: the parallel fraction, the share of the one-worker running time that can be split between workers, from 0 to 1; the finite ceiling below assumes a nonzero serial share, so p is less than 1
1 − p: the serial fraction, the share that must run on one worker whatever happens
S_max: the limit of S(N) as N grows without bound (infinitely many workers): the parallel term p / N shrinks to 0
In words: extra workers shorten only the work that can run in parallel. The serial work remains, so it eventually dominates and limits the benefit of adding workers.
```

For example, if 5% of the original job is serial, even unlimited workers cannot make the fixed job more than twenty times faster. This assumes the parallel part splits perfectly with no coordination overhead; real overhead can reduce the benefit further.

| Parallel share | Max speed-up |
|---|---|
| 50% | 2x |
| 90% | 10x |
| 95% | 20x |
| 99% | 100x |

With 95% parallel, the ideal speed-up approaches a twentyfold limit as workers increase. For an entirely parallel job, this ideal model has no serial floor; practical communication and resource limits still apply.

In system design, a shared bottleneck may play a similar limiting role. These components are not necessarily single-threaded, but each has finite capacity:

- A single primary database that handles all writes.
- A global lock or a single-threaded sequencer.
- A single coordinator service.

Amdahl tells you that adding app servers won't help once you're bottlenecked on one of these. You must remove or partition the serial component.

> [!note] Universal Scalability Law
> Real systems often do worse than Amdahl, because nodes must coordinate (cache coherence, cross-node chatter). Neil Gunther's USL models two costs: **contention** (queueing for a shared resource, which is Amdahl's serial part) and **coherence** (nodes keeping each other up to date). Coherence cost grows roughly with the number of node *pairs*, which grows much faster than the number of nodes (illustrated below), so it can make throughput *fall* as you add nodes.
>
> The shapes are diagnostic. A curve that rises then **flattens** points to contention: find the shared bottleneck. A curve that rises then **falls** points to coherence: look for all-to-all chatter, global locks or broadcast cache invalidation.

With eight nodes there are 28 distinct pairs; with sixteen there are 120. Doubling the nodes creates more than four times as many possible pairwise relationships in this example. If each node talks to every other on each update, coordination can grow faster than useful work.

Gustafson's law gives the optimistic counterpart: as you add machines you usually also grow the *problem* (more users, more data), so the parallel portion grows and scaling stays useful.

## Scaling the different tiers

| Tier | Typical scaling approach |
|---|---|
| Static content | CDN |
| Stateless app | Horizontal + autoscaling |
| Read-heavy data | Cache + read replicas |
| Write-heavy data | Partition (shard) |
| Async work | Queue + worker pool |

Each technique gets its own lesson later. The pattern is consistent: find the bottleneck, apply the technique for that tier, then find the next bottleneck.

## Key takeaways
- For a fixed job, the serial fraction caps speed-up even with unlimited workers.
- Coordination between node pairs can grow much faster than the number of nodes.
- Treat curve shapes as clues, then measure the bottleneck and scale the tier responsible.

## Further reading
- [Amdahl’s law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)
- [Neil Gunther and the Universal Scalability Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_J._Gunther)
- [Little’s Law (Marc Brooker)](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html)
- [Gunther: quantifying scalability](https://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.pdf)

questions.prompt: A fixed batch job contains a serial merge step and a large parallel stage. After adding many workers, the merge dominates the runtime. What is the most useful next improvement?

options.text: Keep doubling workers indefinitely
options.explanation: Incorrect. Extra workers shorten only the parallel stage; they cannot remove the unchanged serial merge.

options.text: Treat the serial merge as free because it was small initially
options.explanation: Incorrect. Its absolute time remains as the parallel stage shrinks.

options.text: Assume every worker adds the same speed-up forever
options.explanation: Incorrect. Fixed serial work causes diminishing returns even before coordination overhead.

options.text: Reduce or restructure the serial merge, then remeasure the whole job
options.explanation: Correct. Once serial work dominates, improving it can help more than adding parallel capacity.

questions.workedExample: Imagine the parallel stage becoming almost instantaneous. The merge still remains. This thought experiment exposes the floor on runtime for a fixed job. Profile the serial work and consider a different merge structure; measure coordination overhead and correctness before assuming the new structure scales.

questions.prompt: You add app servers to a service that writes every request to a single Postgres primary. Throughput rises from 1 to 4 servers, then flattens from 4 to 16; monitoring shows the primary saturating while the other tiers have headroom. What's the most likely explanation?

options.text: The single write primary is now the serial bottleneck, so more app servers can't help
options.explanation: Correct. This is Amdahl's law in practice: once the shared primary is saturated, it's the serial component. Options include batching writes, scaling the primary up, removing unnecessary writes, or partitioning the data.

options.text: The load balancer has a maximum of 4 backends
options.explanation: Incorrect. Production load balancers handle hundreds or thousands of backends. If this were the cause, the extra servers simply wouldn't receive traffic, which you'd see immediately.

options.text: The app servers need more RAM
options.explanation: Incorrect. If each app server were the bottleneck, adding more would keep increasing throughput. The flat curve shows the limit is something they all share.

options.text: Horizontal scaling never works for web apps
options.explanation: Incorrect. It worked well from 1 to 4 servers. The plateau is caused by a specific shared bottleneck, not by horizontal scaling in general.

questions.workedExample:
Read the curve:

```
servers: 1    2    4    8    16
req/s:   1k   2k   4k   4.2k 4.3k
```

Linear growth then a plateau means a **shared** resource saturated at about 4,000 req/s. Each request needs one write on the primary, so the primary caps throughput at about 4,000 writes/s however many app servers sit in front.

Diagnose: primary CPU, I/O or lock waits near 100% at the plateau.
Fix: reduce writes per request, batch, scale the primary vertically, or shard writes across several primaries.

questions.prompt: A cluster's throughput is 10k req/s with 4 nodes, 18k with 8, and **15k with 16**. Every node broadcasts cache invalidations to every other node on each write; for the scaling thought experiment, per-node write generation remains fixed as nodes are added. What best explains the curve?

options.text: Amdahl's law: a serial component caps throughput
options.explanation: Incorrect. Pure contention makes throughput flatten towards a ceiling. It never makes throughput *fall* when you add nodes.

options.text: All-to-all coordination overhead grows faster than capacity and can eventually reduce throughput
options.explanation: Correct. With 16 nodes there are 120 node pairs, against 28 with 8 nodes. Coordination work grows faster than capacity, so the curve goes retrograde.

options.text: The load balancer is the bottleneck at 18k req/s
options.explanation: Incorrect. A simple fixed-capacity load-balancer model predicts a plateau, but real load balancers can also incur backend-dependent overhead; the specified all-to-all work is the strongest clue here.

options.text: The new nodes are faulty
options.explanation: Incorrect. Possible, but the scenario names a mechanism (all-to-all broadcasts) whose cost grows with the square of the node count. That's the systematic explanation.

questions.workedExample: Each new node both adds capacity and creates more communication partners. With per-node write generation fixed and broadcasts to every peer, coordination work grows faster than the node count. That mechanism fits the measured fall in throughput. Check invalidation volume and resource waits, then consider ownership by key, narrower invalidation or a shared log. A falling curve is a clue, not proof of a cause on its own.

link.title: Neil J. Gunther and the Universal Scalability Law (Wikipedia)

questions.prompt: A fixed pipeline has a small serial stage. A capacity model says extra workers can meet today's speed-up goal, but a more ambitious goal lies beyond the serial-stage limit. Which plan is sound?

options.text: Buy enough workers and the serial-stage limit disappears
options.explanation: Incorrect. More workers do not shorten work that still runs serially.

options.text: Use measured workers for the reachable goal and redesign serial work for the larger goal
options.explanation: Correct. Worker count and serial work address different constraints; coordination overhead must also be measured.

options.text: Reject all parallelism because one stage is serial
options.explanation: Incorrect. Parallel work can still provide useful speed-up below the limit.

options.text: Grow the job's input until the original fixed-job target is met
options.explanation: Incorrect. Changing problem size does not demonstrate the required speed-up for the original job.

questions.workedExample: For the same fixed input, additional workers divide the parallel work while the serial stage remains. First verify whether the practical target fits beneath that floor, including overhead. A target beyond it requires reducing the serial work or changing the algorithm, rather than solving for a larger worker count.

questions.prompt: A product catalogue gets about 100 reads for every write, and its single database is struggling under the **read** load. What is the usual first step?

options.text: Add a cache in front of the database and read replicas behind it
options.explanation: Correct. The tier table matches read-heavy data with caching and read replicas. If the measured working set is cacheable, hits reduce database reads and replicas can serve eligible misses, while writes stay on one simple primary.

options.text: Shard the database by product ID
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sharding spreads writes and data, but it's complex and the problem here is reads, which have cheaper fixes.

options.text: Put the database behind a CDN
options.explanation: Incorrect. CDNs serve static or cacheable HTTP content at the edge. They don't sit in front of a database's query interface.

options.text: Add more stateless app servers
options.explanation: Incorrect. The app servers aren't the bottleneck; more of them would just send more queries to the struggling database.

questions.workedExample:
Match the technique to the bottleneck:

| Bottleneck | Technique |
|---|---|
| Static content | CDN |
| Stateless app CPU | More app servers |
| Read-heavy data | Cache + replicas |
| Write-heavy data | Sharding |

At 100:1, a cache with a 90% hit rate removes 90% of database reads in one step. Replicas then absorb the misses. Sharding is reserved for when writes or data size outgrow one primary.

lessons.title: Size concurrency pools with Little’s law
lessons.summary: Connect resource-holding time with concurrency, and predict why a slow dependency exhausts a pool.
lessons.body:
Thread and connection pools limit how many requests can hold a resource at once. Little’s law estimates their average occupancy and shows what changes when a downstream call becomes slow.

## Little's law: concurrency, throughput, latency

Little's law is one of the most useful equations in capacity planning. For any stable system (one where the queue doesn't grow forever), averaged over a long enough time:

```formula reference
L = λ × W
where
L: the average number of items in the system at once (requests in flight, busy threads, open connections); a plain count
λ: lambda, the average arrival rate, which in a stable system equals the throughput, in items per second (/s)
W: the average time each item spends inside the system, in seconds (s)
s: second
In words: at a stable arrival rate, keeping each request inside longer means more requests are present at once. Use the time spent holding the particular resource when estimating its average occupancy.
```

It holds regardless of arrival distribution, and applies to a single thread pool, a whole service or a coffee shop.

**Example 1: sizing a thread pool.** A service handles 2,000 req/s, and each request spends 50 ms in the service (much of it waiting on the database):

This workload keeps about **100 requests in flight on average**. With one occupied thread per request, that means about 100 busy threads before headroom.

**Example 2: database connections.** 5,000 queries/s at 4 ms each:

About **20 connections are busy on average**. This uses connection-holding time, not the whole request duration.

A pool of 30–40 is a starting hypothesis, not a guarantee: burstiness, latency tails and database capacity determine the necessary headroom. A pool of 500 per app instance across 50 instances permits 25,000 connections and can impose substantial overhead; validate the total against database capacity rather than assuming more connections help.

**Example 3: what happens when latency rises.** The database slows from 4 ms to 40 ms while traffic stays at 5,000/s:

Average connection demand would rise to about **200** if the same throughput could be maintained. That is ten times the previous occupancy.

The pool of 40 is exhausted; requests queue, latency rises further, and the problem cascades. Little's law explains why a slow dependency causes thread or connection-pool exhaustion upstream, and why timeouts and bulkheads (reliability module) matter.

## Key takeaways
- Average concurrency equals average arrival rate multiplied by average time inside a stable system.
- Use the time spent holding the resource you are sizing, with seconds matching the per-second rate.
- Longer resource occupancy requires more concurrency; pool headroom and database capacity must be measured.

## Further reading
- [Little’s Law (Marc Brooker)](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html)
- [Handling Overload (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

questions.prompt: A stable service keeps about 30 database connections busy on average. Why is configuring exactly 30 connections without further measurement risky?

options.text: A larger pool always improves the database's throughput
options.explanation: Incorrect. Excess connections can add contention and overhead; database capacity still limits useful concurrency.

options.text: Average occupancy already includes the worst burst
options.explanation: Incorrect. An average does not describe peak or tail occupancy.

options.text: Bursts and variable holding times can exhaust the pool; test headroom against database capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Little's law relates averages and does not supply a safe pool maximum by itself.

options.text: Only total HTTP duration matters, even if connections are released much earlier
options.explanation: Incorrect. Connection sizing uses the time the connection is held, rather than unrelated request work.

questions.workedExample: Use Little's law to estimate average resource occupancy, then separate it from a capacity decision. Measure bursts, latency tails and how long connections are held. Check the total across all app instances against what the database can sustain before choosing headroom.

questions.prompt: A service uses one thread per request. A downstream dependency becomes much slower while arrivals stay unchanged, and the caller's fixed-size thread pools had only modest spare capacity. What is the likely failure mechanism?

options.text: Nothing changes because incoming traffic has not increased
options.explanation: Incorrect. Longer request-holding time increases the concurrency needed at the same throughput.

options.text: The service autoscales out of trouble immediately
options.explanation: Incorrect. Autoscaling may not react quickly enough, and extra instances add more load to the already-degraded dependency. Timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads are the proper defence.

options.text: Threads are released immediately whenever the dependency is slow
options.explanation: Incorrect. In this blocking design, a request occupies its thread while waiting.

options.text: More threads remain occupied, pools fill, and excess requests queue or fail
options.explanation: Correct. Resource holding time increased without an equivalent increase in capacity, so the caller can exhaust its pools.

questions.workedExample: Follow a thread: it remains occupied until its slow call finishes or times out. At unchanged arrivals, longer occupancy requires more threads to maintain throughput. Once the pool fills, further work waits or is rejected; the old throughput cannot simply be assumed stable. Bound waiting, set appropriate timeouts, isolate dependency pools and shed load. Extra callers can worsen the downstream overload.

lessons.title: Keep units and orders of magnitude straight
lessons.summary: Convert daily counts, powers of ten and network bits into consistent estimation units.
lessons.body:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is quick, approximate arithmetic that tells you **which order of magnitude** you're dealing with. Is this one database or a hundred? Gigabytes or petabytes? One server or a fleet?

The goal is not precision. Being within a factor of 2–3 is fine. Being off by 1,000x because you confused MB with GB is not.

## Reference units, not a memory test

### Large counts and time

Use thousand, million and billion consistently. Moving between decimal size prefixes changes the scale by a thousand each step. Write the units beside estimates so a missed prefix is visible.

For daily counts, a day contains 86,400 seconds. Dividing a count per day by that duration gives an **average** per-second rate, not the busiest-second demand. A 365.25-day year contains about 31.6 million seconds; rounded estimates should say which convention they use.

| Daily events | Average events/s |
|---|---|
| 1 million | About 12 |
| 10 million | About 120 |
| 100 million | About 1,200 |
| 1 billion | About 12,000 |

Use these as a scale check, then allow for the measured traffic peak.

### Size

| Unit | Bytes | In words |
|---|---|---|
| KB (kilobyte) | 1,000 | thousand |
| MB (megabyte) | 1,000,000 | million |
| GB (gigabyte) | 10 to the power 9 | billion |
| TB (terabyte) | 10 to the power 12 | trillion |
| PB (petabyte) | 10 to the power 15 | quadrillion |

Each step up the table is 1,000 times bigger. (Using powers of 10 rather than powers of 2 introduces an error of about 2% at KB, growing to about 13% at PB: a binary kilobyte is 1,024 bytes, 2.4% more than 1,000. That's fine for estimates. Strictly, the binary units are KiB, MiB, GiB and so on.)

### Illustrative object-size assumptions

These are exercise inputs, not measured universal sizes. Content gap: no representative dataset is provided for a reliable generic object-size table; measure your own serialized records and media.

| Item | Assumed size |
|---|---|
| ID / timestamp | 8 bytes |
| Short text post + metadata | 300 B – 1 KB |
| User profile row | 1 KB |
| Compressed photo | 200 KB – 2 MB |
| 1 minute of HD video | ~40–100 MB |

### Bandwidth

Network speeds are quoted in bits per second; storage and file sizes in bytes.

A byte contains **eight bits**. A 1 Gbps link therefore has a raw rate equivalent to 125 MB/s, and a 10 Gbps link to 1.25 GB/s. Application throughput is lower once protocol overhead and other limits are included. A claim that a 10 Gbps link sends 10 GB/s confuses bits with bytes.

## Key takeaways
- Estimate the order of magnitude and state what you rounded.
- Daily counts become average per-second rates by dividing by 86,400 seconds.
- Distinguish decimal and binary sizes, and divide bits by eight to obtain bytes.
- Object sizes in the table are illustrative assumptions; measure the records and media you will store.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Back-of-the-envelope calculation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back-of-the-envelope_calculation)
- [NIST: decimal and binary prefixes](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html)

questions.prompt: An estimate converts a daily event total into an average events-per-second rate. What must be checked before using that rate to provision servers?

options.text: Whether the average has enough decimal places
options.explanation: Incorrect. More precision does not reveal bursts or a workload's actual capacity.

options.text: Whether each server's CPU count matches the number of daily users
options.explanation: Incorrect. A user total alone is not resource demand.

options.text: Nothing; the daily average already represents every second
options.explanation: Incorrect. Daily totals can hide concentrated demand.

options.text: The traffic's peak shape and sustainable capacity at the required latency
options.explanation: Correct. An average rate is a scale estimate, while the fleet must satisfy the chosen peak and service targets.

questions.workedExample: Dividing by the seconds in the day spreads events evenly. Real demand may concentrate into a launch, commute or on-sale period. State the peak assumption, measure the workload, and check survivor capacity instead of treating a smooth average as a guarantee.

questions.prompt: A capacity document treats a 10 Gbps network card as 10 GB/s of application data. What is the main error?

options.text: It assumes bits and bytes represent the same quantity at the same numeric rate
options.explanation: Correct. A byte contains eight bits. The raw equivalent is 1.25 GB/s before protocol overhead and other bottlenecks.

options.text: It should multiply the gigabit rate by eight to obtain gigabytes per second
options.explanation: Incorrect. A byte groups eight bits, so the numeric byte rate is smaller.

options.text: Network speed determines database durability
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability depends on the persistence and acknowledgement contract, not the network-card label.

options.text: There is no error because both prefixes mean billion
options.explanation: Incorrect. The prefix is the same scale, but bit and byte are different units.

questions.workedExample: Read the unit as well as the prefix: Gbps counts billions of bits each second, while GB/s counts billions of bytes. Correct the conversion, then treat the raw rate as an upper bound rather than promised application throughput. Protocol overhead, CPU, storage and congestion can lower useful delivery.

link.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know (gist)

questions.prompt: A service's steady write rate stays unchanged, but retention changes from one month to one year. What happens to raw retained storage, before replication?

options.text: It stays the same because the per-second rate is unchanged
options.explanation: Incorrect. An unchanged rate accumulates more data when kept longer.

options.text: It falls because older records become cheaper automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Cheaper tiers are a separate policy; retention alone does not shrink the raw bytes.

options.text: It depends only on the number of app servers
options.explanation: Incorrect. Retained record volume is driven by write rate, record size and time kept.

options.text: It grows roughly with retention duration, assuming record sizes and deletion behaviour stay unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping the same stream for longer retains more records.

questions.workedExample: Separate a rate from an accumulated quantity. The service produces bytes each second; retention determines how many seconds of production remain stored. State the duration and units, then add the actual replication and storage overhead. A per-day result cannot be reused as a per-year result.

lessons.title: Estimate request rates, records and cache memory
lessons.summary: Separate peak traffic, retained copies and a measured cache hot set before choosing capacity.
lessons.body:
With the units established, use a sequence of explicit assumptions and small calculations. A URL shortener demonstrates why read traffic, stored records and cache memory need separate estimates.

## The method

1. **State assumptions:** active users, actions per user, measured record size, retention and copies.
2. **Separate average from peak traffic.** A daily total hides bursts; choose a peak factor from the actual traffic shape.
3. **Count retained data and copies.** Longer retention and more full replicas both increase storage.
4. **Estimate delivered bytes separately.** Reading an item many times adds delivery traffic without creating new stored records.
5. **Measure the cache hot set.** Count distinct keys needed for the intended hit rate, then include memory overhead.
6. **Check the design implication.** Compare each resource demand with a benchmark of the intended workload.

A useful reference for record storage is:

```formula reference
V = N_day × z × t × r
where
V: raw replicated record storage, in bytes
N_day: new records per day
z: bytes per record
t: retention in days
r: number of full copies
In words: storage grows with the daily number of records, each record's size, how long records are retained and how many copies are kept. Indexes, metadata and free-space headroom add to this raw estimate.
```

## A URL shortener: what matters

Assume **100 million new links a month**, **100 redirects per new link**, roughly **500 bytes per record**, **ten years of retention**, and a **threefold peak factor**. These are exercise inputs.

Using a rounded 2.5 million seconds per month gives about 40 writes/s and 4,000 reads/s on average. The assumed peak gives about 120 writes/s and 12,000 reads/s. Reads dominate, so a cache or read replicas may help; a large lifetime record count does not by itself prove the write path needs sharding.

Ten years gives twelve billion records: about **6 TB for one copy** and **18 TB for three**, before indexes, metadata, backups and headroom. Shorter retention changes that storage budget without necessarily changing today's peak traffic.

For cache memory, suppose access traces identify **80 million distinct hot links**. Their raw payload is about **40 GB** at the assumed record size. Add Redis object/index overhead, replication and spare memory before choosing nodes. Total requests or an assumed 80/20 rule cannot establish the number of distinct keys needed for a desired hit rate.

These rates are candidates for a straightforward database-and-cache design. Benchmark the actual queries, contention and durability settings before choosing capacity. The estimate directs attention to read load, retained data, ID generation and availability; it does not certify that one particular database deployment will suffice.

## Key takeaways
- Calculate average traffic, apply an explicit peak factor, then estimate storage, bandwidth and hot-set memory.
- Retention and replication multiply record storage; cache payload still needs overhead and headroom.
- A hot-set size comes from distinct-key access measurements, not total requests or an assumed 80/20 rule.
- Finish with design implications and a workload-specific capacity check.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Fermi problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermi_problem)

questions.prompt: A message-store estimate includes today's daily message bytes but omits five-year retention and three full replicas. Why is it too small?

options.text: It counts only one day's one-copy payload instead of all retained copies
options.explanation: Correct. Retention determines how many days remain stored, and full replication stores each retained record more than once.

options.text: Replication reduces the logical message size
options.explanation: Incorrect. Copies improve redundancy; they do not compress the original payload.

options.text: Daily active users must all be connected simultaneously
options.explanation: Incorrect. Active-user counts and simultaneous connections are different quantities.

options.text: Every stored byte must also be counted as an app-server CPU core
options.explanation: Incorrect. Storage volume and CPU work are different resource demands.

questions.workedExample: Identify what the estimate represents: one day and one copy. Ask how many days remain under the retention policy and how many full copies are stored. Then include indexes, metadata, backups and headroom as the design requires. A large result should prompt placement and capacity checks, not automatically select a particular database.

questions.prompt: A news-site estimate starts with page views per day. Each page triggers several API calls, and the busy period is much heavier than the average. What must the API capacity estimate account for?

options.text: Only the number of pages; API calls do not consume capacity separately
options.explanation: Incorrect. Multiple calls per page can multiply backend demand.

options.text: Only average API traffic, because bursts average out eventually
options.explanation: Incorrect. The service must handle the required peak while it occurs.

options.text: The number of bytes in a database backup alone
options.explanation: Incorrect. Backup size does not determine request-processing demand.

options.text: Calls per page and the measured peak factor, with daily and per-second units kept consistent
options.explanation: Correct. Both request amplification and traffic shape affect the peak demand.

questions.workedExample: Trace one user action into backend operations, then convert the total into a rate using consistent time units. Distinguish the average from peak demand. Finally compare the resulting workload with measured per-server capacity and failure headroom.

questions.prompt: You are sizing a profile cache. Access traces identify the distinct keys needed for the intended hit rate. What should the RAM estimate include?

options.text: Only serialized profile payloads, with memory filled completely
options.explanation: Incorrect. Entries have implementation overhead and the cache needs operational headroom.

options.text: Every registered user's profile, regardless of access patterns
options.explanation: Incorrect. A useful cache can target a measured hot set rather than all historical users.

options.text: The measured hot set, per-entry overhead and headroom, with replica memory accounted for separately
options.explanation: Correct. The raw hot-set payload is only one part of total provisioned memory.

options.text: The total number of daily requests treated as distinct profiles
options.explanation: Incorrect. Many requests may access the same key; requests do not determine distinct-key count.

questions.workedExample: Begin with distinct keys needed for the target hit rate, not daily request totals. Measure entry memory for the actual representation, include spare memory and count replicas. Validate warm-up, expiry, eviction and hit rate under realistic traces. Daily active users alone do not guarantee a cache hit rate.

lessons.title: Estimate media storage and delivery bandwidth
lessons.summary: Explain why media can dominate storage, repeated delivery drives egress, and simultaneous viewers determine streaming demand.
lessons.body:
The preceding record estimate is only part of a media service. Large objects and repeated delivery can dominate the storage and network budget even when the metadata database is modest.

## A social feed: separate metadata from media

Assume 200 million daily active users, each posting twice and viewing 100 posts daily. Ten per cent of posts contain a 500 KB photo; text and metadata take about 1 KB per post. These are exercise inputs, with decimal size units.

Using a rounded 100,000 seconds per day gives about **4,000 posts/s** and **200,000 post views/s** on average. An assumed threefold peak raises these to about 12,000 and 600,000 respectively. The read-heavy pattern makes caching and precomputation candidates, subject to freshness and fan-out costs.

The important storage result is the imbalance:

| One-copy payload | Per day | Per 365-day year |
|---|---|---|
| Text and metadata | 400 GB | About 150 TB |
| Photos | 20 TB | About 7.3 PB |

Photos dominate even though they occur in a minority of posts. Keeping large media in object storage and keeping references and searchable metadata in the database is a useful starting design; the estimate does not require every byte to live in a database disk.

## Delivered bytes differ from stored bytes

Assume ten per cent of the 20 billion daily views fetch a photo. That delivers about **1 PB per day**, or roughly **80 Gbps** using the same rounded day. A photo stored once can be downloaded many times, so upload volume alone cannot size egress.

A CDN can serve repeat requests near users and reduce origin traffic. Its cache hit rate changes how much delivery load reaches the origin; it does not remove the bytes users receive. Measure geography, cacheability, payload sizes and peak demand.

> [!tip] Say what an estimate changes
