> A large result should lead to a resource or architecture question: where are the objects stored, which traffic can an edge cache serve, and can the origin survive misses? It should not automatically lead to sharding the metadata database.

## A streaming service: concurrency matters

Assume **one million concurrent viewers**, each consuming an average **5 Mbps** stream. Their combined peak delivery is **5 Tbps**, equivalent to **625 GB/s**. These assumed values explain why delivery placement and bandwidth can dominate a streaming design.

The number of viewers watching at once matters here, rather than daily active users or uploads. Higher bitrate or more simultaneous viewers raises delivery demand directly. Provision measured server capacity with headroom and geographic redundancy; one generic network-card rate cannot determine the fleet. Netflix's Open Connect places delivery appliances inside ISP networks to serve traffic close to viewers.

## Key takeaways
- Photos can dominate storage even when only a small share of posts contain them.
- Estimate media bytes delivered as well as bytes retained, with bits and bytes kept distinct.
- A CDN supports offload, geography and redundancy; assumed NIC rates need workload-specific validation.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Netflix Open Connect](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)

questions.prompt: A colleague estimates 2 TB of photo uploads per day and concludes: "A 4 TB database disk lasts two days, so we need to shard Postgres." Assume the daily payload estimate is correct. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.text: At this scale, consider object storage for photo blobs and keep metadata in the database before deciding to shard
options.explanation: Correct. Keeping large media in object storage and references and searchable metadata in the database separates two different storage and access workloads. The metadata database still needs measured capacity checks.

options.text: The estimate ignores replication of the stored photos
options.explanation: Correct. Physical storage planning must include the chosen replication or erasure-coding scheme; managed object-storage billing may already include that redundancy. It doesn't change the conclusion about where to store them, but it's a real omission.

options.text: The arithmetic is wrong: 1 M × 2 MB is 2 GB
options.explanation: Incorrect. The stated daily photo payload of 2 TB is correct using decimal units. The questionable step is treating all photo bytes as database-disk growth.

options.text: The estimate doesn't consider multiple resized versions (thumbnails) per photo
options.explanation: Correct. Most photo apps store several renditions (thumbnail, medium, full). Thumbnails are small, but they add storage and, more importantly, they're what most reads fetch, which affects CDN and bandwidth planning.

questions.workedExample: Accept the stated payload total, then challenge where the bytes belong. Object storage with CDN delivery is a useful starting point for photo objects, while a database stores references and metadata. Include measured rendition sizes and the actual redundancy policy, remembering that managed-service pricing may already include redundant storage. Check retention, queries, backups and maintenance before deciding whether the metadata database needs sharding.

questions.prompt: A video platform knows its average uploaded bytes per day. A colleague uses that alone to size peak network capacity for both uploads and playback. What is missing?

options.text: Nothing; ingress and playback always carry identical volumes
options.explanation: Incorrect. Stored videos can be played repeatedly and uploads can be bursty.

options.text: Only the database's number of columns
options.explanation: Incorrect. Schema alone does not determine upload or streaming network demand.

options.text: Peak upload shape plus simultaneous playback demand and bitrate, with bits and bytes kept distinct
options.explanation: Correct. Average ingress, peak ingress and playback egress are different demands.

options.text: Only the number of videos ever uploaded
options.explanation: Incorrect. A historical count does not reveal current upload or viewing rates.

questions.workedExample: Separate the directions. Ingress receives new objects; egress repeatedly delivers them to viewers. A daily total gives an average only after choosing a time unit. Peak viewing depends on simultaneous viewers and stream bitrate, while upload peaks require their own measured traffic shape.

lessons.title: Turn workload estimates into a resilient fleet
lessons.summary: Use CPU time and concurrency to size capacity, then account for replicas, overhead, peaks and zone failure.
lessons.body:
A traffic estimate becomes a fleet estimate only after you specify what consumes each resource. CPU work, concurrent connections and replicated writes are different constraints, and failure removes usable capacity.

## Worked example 4: servers needed

**Assumptions:** 50,000 req/s peak, each request uses ~20 ms of CPU, servers have 16 cores, target 60% utilisation.

```formula reference
n_s = (Q × t_cpu) / (c × u)
where
n_s: server count before adding failure redundancy; round up to whole servers
Q: peak requests per second
t_cpu: measured CPU time per request, in seconds
c: CPU cores per server
u: target CPU utilisation as a fraction, such as 0.6 for 60%
In words: compare the CPU work arriving each second with the work one server can do at the chosen utilisation. Then check memory, I/O, latency and survivor capacity separately.
```

These assumptions require about 105 servers before zone redundancy. If three evenly sized zones must survive losing one, the two remaining zones together need that capacity. Rounding to 53 servers per zone gives **159 servers total**. This is an illustrative CPU estimate, not a guarantee about I/O, memory or tail latency.

## Common pitfalls

- **Bits vs bytes.** Network speeds are in bits; storage is in bytes. A 1 Gbps raw link rate corresponds to 125 MB/s before overhead.
- **Forgetting peaks.** Average QPS sizes nothing; capacity must handle the peak.
- **Forgetting concurrency.** For connections and sessions, use Little's law: the number connected at once is the arrival rate multiplied by the time each stays online. For example, 50 million daily users connected for 30 minutes each implies about one million connections on average, before the peak factor.
- **Forgetting replication and overhead.** Three replicas triple storage; index and metadata overhead depends on the schema and storage engine; state an explicit allowance or measure it.
- **Forgetting growth.** Plan for at least the next 1–2 years.
- **False precision.** "4,629.6 QPS" signals you've missed the point. Say "about 5k".

> [!warning] Check your units at every step
> Write the unit next to every number. Most estimation errors are unit errors, not arithmetic errors.

## Key takeaways
- CPU-seconds arriving per second estimate busy cores; target utilisation determines usable capacity per server.
- Size the survivors for peak traffic when a whole zone fails, then provision the complete fleet.
- Connections require concurrency estimates, while replicated writes consume capacity on every required copy.
- Include units, peaks, overhead and growth; avoid false precision.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Little’s Law (Marc Brooker)](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html)
- [Handling Overload (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

questions.prompt: A CPU-based fleet estimate meets peak load only while all three equally sized zones are healthy. The service must survive losing one zone at the same target utilisation. What should change?

options.text: Provision enough in the two surviving zones to carry the full peak workload
options.explanation: Correct. Size the survivor capacity first, then build all three zones to the required per-zone capacity.

options.text: Keep the same fleet because the load balancer can create CPU capacity
options.explanation: Incorrect. Routing redistributes work; it cannot replace the lost resources.

options.text: Count every CPU core as usable at full saturation and ignore the latency target
options.explanation: Incorrect. The target utilisation and measured latency are part of the capacity requirement.

options.text: Add replicas without checking where their capacity is placed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Capacity lost with the failed zone cannot help survivors.

questions.workedExample: List the resources remaining after a zone loss and compare them with peak demand at the chosen utilisation. Round whole servers within each zone, then check total placement. CPU estimates also need memory, I/O and latency validation; zone headroom cannot be inferred from a healthy fleet total alone.

link.title: Static stability using Availability Zones (Amazon Builders' Library)

questions.prompt: You review a colleague's capacity estimate. The storage design uses three full replicas with an assumed 20–50% per-copy index/metadata overhead. Which of these steps are **errors** that need fixing? Select all that apply.

options.text: Converted a 1 Gbps link to 1 GB/s of capacity
options.explanation: Correct, this is an error. 1 Gbps is 125 MB/s. Treating it as 1 GB/s overstates capacity eightfold.

options.text: Sized the database cluster for average QPS
options.explanation: Correct, this is an error. Peak demand and failure headroom must be explicit; a daily average does not establish the busiest period's capacity.

options.text: Rounded 86,400 seconds per day to 100,000
options.explanation: Not an error. This is a standard simplification, about 16% off, and well within the factor-of-2–3 tolerance of an estimate.

options.text: Treated 6 TB of raw records as needing 6 TB of disk
options.explanation: Correct, this is an error. Three full replicas and the stated per-copy overhead require more than the single-copy raw record payload. Actual allowances must follow the storage design.

options.text: Reported the result as "about 5k QPS" rather than "4,629.6 QPS"
options.explanation: Not an error. Rounding to a sensible figure is the right presentation; false precision misleads.

questions.workedExample: Audit dimensions and assumptions before checking arithmetic. A bit rate cannot be relabelled as the same byte rate. Average traffic cannot stand in for the chosen peak. A one-copy payload cannot represent three replicas plus indexes and metadata. Rounding is useful when declared and small enough for the decision; excessive decimal places do not make uncertain assumptions accurate.

questions.prompt: A connection-service estimate divides daily active users by each server's connection limit, assuming every daily user is online at once. What is the better approach?

options.text: Use all daily users as peak connections in every product
options.explanation: Incorrect. That can greatly overstate concurrency; it is a separate worst-case assumption, not an implication of DAU.

options.text: Use only average connections and ignore peaks
options.explanation: Incorrect. Average occupancy does not guarantee peak capacity.

options.text: Estimate simultaneous connections from time online and arrivals, measure the peak, then add headroom and failure capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Connection servers are limited by what is held concurrently, not the total users seen over a day.

options.text: Mix time online in minutes with arrivals per second without converting
options.explanation: Incorrect. Time units must match when estimating occupancy.

questions.workedExample: Ask how many users overlap in time. A user present briefly and one connected all day impose different average occupancy despite each counting once in DAU. Use a consistent time basis and the relevant connection-holding duration, then validate peak connections, memory, traffic and reconnect behaviour during failures.

questions.prompt: A time-series store copies every logical write to three nodes. An estimate divides incoming logical writes by a measured per-node write rate but counts each write only once. What is the error?

options.text: The node count should ignore replication because the client sends once
options.explanation: Incorrect. Client request count and total replica work are different.

options.text: The estimate omits the work performed on the additional replicas
options.explanation: Correct. Every required copy consumes capacity; the per-node benchmark must match the intended replication workload.

options.text: Replication makes each stored reading disappear after acknowledgement
options.explanation: Incorrect. Replication creates copies rather than deleting the payload.

options.text: Batching readings necessarily reduces payload bytes in the same proportion as operation count
options.explanation: Incorrect. A batch can share operation overhead while retaining the same raw readings; benchmark the larger batch.

questions.workedExample: Trace one logical write through the store: the ingest request produces work on each required replica. Size aggregate replica work and its placement, then check survivor capacity. Batching may reduce operation overhead without proportionally reducing bytes, so remeasure throughput for the actual batch size.

lessons.title: Understand CAP through a two-node partition
lessons.summary: Use the exact definitions of linearisability and CAP availability to see why an isolated replica must choose.
lessons.body:
The CAP theorem is the most quoted and most misunderstood result in distributed systems. Used carefully, it's a sharp tool for reasoning about what happens during a network failure. Used loosely ("Mongo is CP, Cassandra is AP"), it mostly causes confusion.

## The precise statement

Eric Brewer conjectured it in 2000; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved it in 2002. In their formulation:

- **C (consistency)** means **linearisability**: every read sees the most recent completed write, as if there were a single copy of the data.
- **A (availability)** means **every request received by a non-failing node must get a non-error response**. No time limit, but no "sorry, try later".
- **P (partition tolerance)** means the system keeps operating even if the network drops arbitrary messages between nodes.

The theorem: **in the presence of a network partition, a system cannot be both linearisable and available.**

## Why it's true: the two-node argument

```
  client X              client Y
     |                     |
     v                     v
 +--------+   //////   +--------+
 | node 1 |<-- cut --->| node 2 |
 |  v = 1 |   //////   |  v = 0 |
 +--------+            +--------+
```

1. Cut the network between the nodes before the write, so node 2 cannot receive it.
2. Client X writes `v = 1` to node 1 and receives a successful acknowledgement before Y starts reading.
3. Client Y reads `v` from node 2.

Node 2 has two choices:

- **Answer with `v = 0`.** It stays available but returns stale data: not linearisable. *Choose A.*
- **Refuse or wait** until it can contact node 1. It stays consistent but isn't available. *Choose C.*

There is no third option. That's the whole theorem.

## Why “pick two of three” misleads

The Venn-diagram version suggests you can pick consistency plus availability, consistency plus partition tolerance, or availability plus partition tolerance like menu items. But **you don't get to choose whether partitions happen**. Networks drop packets, switches fail, GC pauses make nodes unreachable, cloud zones lose connectivity.

So for any system spread over a network, P isn't optional. The real statement is:

> [!note] The useful form
> *When a partition happens*, choose between consistency and availability. *When there's no partition*, you can have both.

A design claiming both consistency and availability by excluding partitions has left that failure case outside its promise. A single node avoids inter-replica partitions, but remains a single point of failure.

## CAP consistency and ACID invariants

They describe different properties.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ACID C | Transactions keep invariants (constraints) valid |
| CAP C | Linearisability: reads see the latest write |

A single-node database can provide linearisable operations, but being single-node does not guarantee that every API or isolation level does so. ACID consistency is a separate question: application logic and constraints must preserve the intended invariants.

## Key takeaways
- During a partition, a replicated system cannot promise both linearisability and successful responses at every non-failing node.
- Partition tolerance is not a menu option that makes network failures disappear.
- CAP consistency concerns operation ordering; ACID consistency concerns application invariants.

## Further reading
- [Brewer’s Conjecture and the Feasibility of CAP](https://users.ece.cmu.edu/~adrian/731-sp04/readings/GL-cap.pdf)
- [CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer)](https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/)
- [Gilbert and Lynch: perspectives on CAP](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf)

questions.prompt: Two replicas cannot communicate. One acknowledges a write; the other receives a later read but has not seen that write. Which statement correctly describes the CAP constraint?

options.text: A distributed system can only ever have two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance
options.explanation: Incorrect. This 'pick two' framing is the common misreading. Partitions aren't something you choose to tolerate; they happen. The trade-off only bites during a partition.

options.text: Strongly consistent databases are always slower than eventually consistent ones
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's closer to the 'else' half of PACELC (latency vs consistency), and even then it's a tendency, not a theorem. CAP says nothing about latency.

options.text: During a network partition, a system must choose between linearisable consistency and availability
options.explanation: Correct. Gilbert and Lynch proved that if the network is partitioned, a node can't both answer every request and guarantee it reflects the latest write. Without a partition, both are possible.

options.text: Relational databases always preserve both consistency and availability; NoSQL databases always sacrifice consistency
options.explanation: Incorrect. CAP doesn't classify database families. A replicated Postgres cluster faces the same partition trade-off as any NoSQL store, and many NoSQL stores (etcd, HBase) prefer consistency.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through the two-node proof:

1. Nodes N1 and N2 replicate key `v` (initially 0).
2. The link between them is cut (partition).
3. A client writes `v = 1` to N1 and receives success before the following read starts.
4. Another client reads `v` from N2.

N2 must either answer `0` (available, not consistent) or refuse/wait (consistent, not available). It can't do both. With no partition, N1 would have replicated to N2 first and both properties hold.

link.title: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of CAP (Gilbert and Lynch, PDF)

questions.prompt: A team says its replica API satisfies CAP consistency because every transaction preserves foreign keys. Which missing guarantee must they investigate?

options.text: Whether later reads reflect completed writes as if there were one copy
options.explanation: Correct. CAP consistency is linearisability, which concerns operation ordering and observed values.

options.text: Whether replicas eventually converge after writes stop
options.explanation: Incorrect. Eventual convergence is weaker than CAP's linearisability requirement.

options.text: Whether the schema uses foreign keys on every table
options.explanation: Incorrect. This concerns database invariants, not the ordering guarantee CAP addresses.

options.text: Whether every replica uses identical field names
options.explanation: Incorrect. A uniform format says nothing about freshness or operation ordering.

questions.workedExample: Preserving constraints is the consistency property described by ACID. CAP asks whether operations behave like a single copy respecting real-time order. A transactionally valid but stale follower read can preserve every foreign key while still violating the latter guarantee.

questions.prompt: A 5-node etcd cluster (Raft) is split by a partition into a group of 3 and a group of 2. A client connected to the 2-node side tries to write. What happens, and how does CAP classify this?

options.text: The write succeeds on the 2-node side and is merged later: AP behaviour
options.explanation: Incorrect. Raft requires a majority (3 of 5) to commit. The 2-node side can't form a majority, so it can't accept writes.

options.text: Both sides accept writes and the higher term wins after healing
options.explanation: Incorrect. That would be split-brain. Raft prevents it precisely by requiring a majority for leadership and commits; terms don't resolve conflicting committed writes.

options.text: The whole cluster stops accepting writes until the partition heals
options.explanation: Incorrect. The 3-node side has a majority, so it can elect a leader and continue committing writes. Only the minority is unavailable.

options.text: The write fails (or blocks) on the minority side; the majority side keeps working: CP behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. Raft sacrifices CAP-availability on the minority side to keep linearisability. The 3-node side elects a leader and continues, so clients that can reach it still succeed.

questions.workedExample: A majority of five is three. The three-node group can elect a leader and commit after the protocol completes; the two-node group cannot get the required votes or acknowledgements. A client that cannot reach the majority therefore cannot complete its write. This sacrifices CAP availability on the minority side while preserving the write-ordering guarantee. Reconnecting clients may restore operational availability, but it does not make every isolated node CAP-available.

link.title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP (Martin Kleppmann)

questions.prompt: From the point of view of the other nodes in a cluster, which of these is **indistinguishable from a network partition**?

options.text: A node is in a 20-second garbage-collection pause
options.explanation: Correct. Peers just see messages go unanswered. They can't tell a paused, slow or crashed node from one cut off by the network, so they must treat it the same way.

options.text: A node returns a value written a second ago
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's a staleness symptom, not a communication failure. The node is responding.

options.text: A node's CPU is at 40% utilisation
options.explanation: Incorrect. A moderately loaded node still answers promptly; nothing looks like lost messages.

options.text: A client sends a malformed request
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's an application error, answered with an error response. Nodes are still communicating.

questions.workedExample:
A partition is defined by what nodes observe: messages between them don't arrive (in time). Ask of each option: *do peers stop hearing from the node?*

| Situation | Peers hear nothing? |
|---|---|
| 20 s GC pause | Yes |
| Stale value | No |
| 40% CPU | No |
| Malformed request | No |

This is why partition handling isn't optional: even inside one datacentre, pauses and overloaded switches produce the same symptoms as a cut cable.

lessons.title: Choose a partition policy and plan reconciliation
lessons.summary: Separate CAP availability from operational uptime, and match refusal or conflict resolution to each data type.
lessons.body:
The CAP proof identifies a constraint; the product still needs a policy. Decide which operations may continue during isolation and what the application must do when connectivity returns.

## CAP availability and operational uptime

CAP availability is extreme: *every* non-failing node must respond successfully, even a node isolated on the minority side of a partition.

Real systems usually mean something weaker by "highly available": most requests succeed most of the time. Systems using **majority quorums** (Raft in etcd, Paxos in Spanner, the similar Zab protocol in ZooKeeper) commonly refuse writes on the minority side during a partition. That consistency-oriented write policy does not establish that every read API is linearisable; ZooKeeper reads, covered below, may be stale. Yet such systems routinely achieve very high availability, because:

- Partitions are relatively rare.
- Clients on the minority side can often fail over to the majority side.

Google Spanner offers a 99.999% monthly uptime commitment for multi-region configurations under its SLA measurement and credit conditions. This can coexist with refusing operations that cannot safely reach the required replicas; the SLA is not a CAP-availability promise.

## Guarantees matter more than labels

Martin Kleppmann's essay "Please stop calling databases CP or AP" makes the case well. Most real systems are **neither** strictly:

- Many offer **tunable** consistency per request. Cassandra lets you pick `ONE`, `QUORUM` or `ALL`; DynamoDB offers eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads.
- Many aren't linearisable even without partitions (e.g. asynchronous replication with reads from replicas), so they don't satisfy CAP's C anyway.
- Many aren't CAP-available either (e.g. a leader-based system where nodes refuse writes when they can't see the leader).

A system that is neither linearisable nor CAP-available is just... a system with other trade-offs. Describe its *actual* guarantees instead: "reads may be up to ~1 s stale", "writes are rejected on the minority side".

## Using this in a design

1. **Decide per data type, not per system.** A bank's balance needs strong consistency; its "recently viewed" list doesn't.
2. **Ask what happens on the minority side of a partition.** Refuse writes? Accept and reconcile later? Serve stale reads with a warning? Brewer's own example is an ATM: during a partition it can keep dispensing cash up to a small limit, accepting a bounded risk and reconciling (and charging overdraft fees) afterwards.
3. **If you choose availability, plan for conflicts.** Last-write-wins (loses data silently), version vectors with application merge, or CRDTs. Amazon's original Dynamo merged conflicting shopping carts, occasionally resurrecting deleted items.
4. **If you choose consistency, plan for unavailability.** Clients need retries, timeouts and clear errors.
5. **Quantify the latency cost.** For an exercise, assume a same-zone quorum takes 1 ms and a cross-region quorum tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Real quorum latency depends on replica placement, protocol and workload; measure it.

The distributed consistency and consensus module covers linearisability, quorums, Raft and conflict resolution in depth.

## Key takeaways
- A majority-quorum system may have high measured uptime while refusing requests on a minority side.
- Choosing to accept partitioned updates requires an application-appropriate conflict-resolution policy.
- Choosing consistency requires client-visible errors, timeouts and recovery behaviour.
- Choose per data type and quantify the latency and business risk of the policy.

## Further reading
- [CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer)](https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/)
- [Eventually Consistent (Werner Vogels)](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html)
- [Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
- [Spanner availability SLA](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/sla)

questions.prompt: An e-commerce shopping cart uses an AP store: during a partition, both sides keep accepting cart updates. When the partition heals, the two versions of a user's cart conflict. Which resolution strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep both versions and merge them, e.g. union of items (as Amazon's Dynamo did) or a CRDT
options.explanation: Correct. Detecting concurrent versions (with version vectors) and merging preserves every add. The known side-effect: a deleted item can reappear, which Amazon judged acceptable since it's better than losing an add. An observed-remove set (OR-Set) preserves removal of observed add-tags, but a concurrent new add survives (add-wins semantics).

options.text: Last-write-wins by timestamp
options.explanation: Incorrect for a cart. LWW silently discards one side's updates (items the user added would vanish), and clock skew can make the 'wrong' write win. It's acceptable only when losing concurrent updates is harmless.

options.text: Reject both versions and empty the cart
options.explanation: Incorrect. This destroys the user's data and defeats the purpose of choosing availability.

options.text: Switch the store to CP so conflicts can't happen
options.explanation: Incorrect as a resolution strategy. A CP store would avoid conflicts but make carts unavailable to users on the minority side during partitions, which is the very trade-off the business rejected by choosing AP.

questions.workedExample:
During a partition:

```
A: {book} + pen -> {book, pen}
B: {book} + mug -> {book, mug}
```

After healing, version vectors show the versions are **concurrent** (neither descends from the other).

- **LWW:** keep {book, mug}, so the pen is lost. Bad.
- **Union merge:** {book, pen, mug}. Every add preserved.

Edge case: if side A removed `book` while B didn't, a naive union brings `book` back. An OR-Set CRDT tags each add with a unique id so removes of observed adds win, avoiding resurrection.

The principle: if you choose A, you must also choose a merge strategy that matches the business semantics.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, a bank's ATMs can't reach the central ledger. Each ATM independently keeps dispensing up to an illustrative £200 per card per day, logs the withdrawals, and settles them when connectivity returns, charging overdraft fees where needed. How is this best described?

options.text: CP: the ATM preserves linearisability of the balance
options.explanation: Incorrect. The ATM approves withdrawals without seeing the latest balance, so two ATMs could both approve against the same funds. That's not linearisable.

options.text: A violation of CAP, because the bank keeps both consistency and availability
options.explanation: Incorrect. The bank doesn't keep linearisable consistency. It accepts temporary inconsistency, which is allowed.

options.text: Both linearisable and CAP-available, because the ATMs and ledger form one system
options.explanation: Incorrect. They communicate over the partitioned network. Being parts of one application does not let them preserve both linearisability and CAP availability during that partition.

options.text: Availability-oriented offline operation with local withdrawal limits and later reconciliation; a global per-card exposure cap needs additional coordination or preallocated rights
options.explanation: Correct. Brewer discusses accepting bounded local risk and reconciling later. But independently disconnected ATMs cannot enforce one shared £200/card/day cap without preallocated spending rights or another coordination mechanism.

questions.workedExample: Each disconnected ATM enforces its own local limit without seeing withdrawals at other ATMs. A card used at several machines can therefore obtain more than one machine's limit in total. The bank accepts that exposure and reconciles later. A true global cap needs a reachable authority or spending rights allocated in advance. The illustrative £200 is an exercise input, not a verified banking policy.

lessons.title: Apply PACELC to everyday replica latency
lessons.summary: Reason about consistency and latency during normal operation, using cross-region writes and local reads.
lessons.body:
CAP alone does not explain the latency paid while every replica is healthy. PACELC asks how replica coordination affects normal reads and writes as well as partition behaviour.

## What CAP leaves out

CAP only talks about behaviour **during a partition**, and only about one consistency model (linearisability) and one extreme availability definition. It says nothing about:

- **Latency**, which you trade against consistency *all the time*, not just during failures.
- Weaker but useful consistency models (causal, read-your-writes, bounded staleness).
- Node crashes, disk failures, or slow nodes (which are indistinguishable from partitions to the other nodes).

That gap is what PACELC fills.

## PACELC

Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC in 2010 (published 2012):

```
# A partition isolates replicas.
if Partition:
    choose Availability or Consistency
# Otherwise, coordination costs latency.
Else (normal operation):
    choose Latency or Consistency
```

The "else" half is the important addition. Even with a healthy network, coordinating replicated data can cost latency. A design that promises acknowledged writes will survive a zone or region loss must place the required copies before confirming them; linearisable reads may also need a leader or quorum. Linearisability alone does not require every write to wait for a distant durable copy: the replication and failure-survival contract matters.

```
 EC: write -> wait for quorum ack
     London --80ms-- Virginia
     latency at least 1 cross-region RTT

 EL: write -> ack locally, replicate
     async; fast but may be stale
```

## Classifying real systems

These are approximate classifications; many are tunable. The table summarises coordination choices, not a promise that every read is linearisable. The next unit explains the read guarantees of Cassandra, etcd and ZooKeeper.

| System | Partition | Else |
|---|---|---|
| Cassandra (ONE reads/writes) | PA-like | EL |
| DynamoDB | Depends on API and global-table consistency mode | Eventual or strong reads |
| Spanner, CockroachDB | PC | EC |
| etcd, ZooKeeper | PC | EC |

- **DynamoDB** reads are eventually consistent by default and cost half as much read capacity as strong reads. `ConsistentRead=true` reflects all prior successful writes and is supported for tables and local secondary indexes, not global secondary indexes or streams. The public read contract does not specify which replica serves the request. Multi-Region eventual-consistency global tables replicate asynchronously across regions, though AWS now also offers a multi-Region strong consistency mode that pays cross-region latency on writes.

- **Spanner** pays commit latency for external consistency, using TrueTime and Paxos across replicas.

## Key takeaways
- PACELC adds the normal-operation trade-off between latency and consistency.
- Cross-region coordination pays network delay even when no partition occurs.
- DynamoDB read options and global-table modes have different contracts; local asynchronous reads can be stale.
- System classifications are approximate; check the API and deployment you will actually use.

## Further reading
- [Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)
- [DynamoDB read consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html)
- [CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer)](https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/)
- [DynamoDB global-table modes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html)

questions.prompt: Your database runs in a single region with no network problems at all. Why might you still choose eventually consistent reads?

options.text: CAP forces you to give up consistency even without partitions
options.explanation: Incorrect. CAP only constrains behaviour during a partition. Without one, you can have both consistency and availability.

options.text: Eventually consistent reads are more durable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Read consistency doesn't affect durability; durability depends on how writes are persisted and replicated.

options.text: Eventually consistent reads can offer lower latency or cost, illustrating the else trade-off in PACELC
options.explanation: Correct. Strong reads must enforce the API's latest-write ordering, sometimes by contacting a leader or quorum. Eventually consistent reads may use nearby replicas with less coordination. DynamoDB, for example, charges strongly consistent reads at twice the capacity of eventually consistent ones.

options.text: Strongly consistent reads aren't possible in a single region
options.explanation: Incorrect. Strong reads are perfectly possible in a single region; DynamoDB, Postgres primary reads and etcd all provide them.

questions.workedExample: No partition is needed for this choice. A replica may answer locally before receiving every recent write, reducing coordination but permitting stale data. For DynamoDB's ordinary provisioned reads, eventual reads use half the read capacity of strong reads for the same item size. Choose the actual API contract and whether stale descriptions are acceptable; strong reads are supported on tables and local secondary indexes, not global secondary indexes or streams.

questions.prompt: Which statements about CAP and PACELC are **correct**? Select all that apply.

options.text: A correctly implemented single-node database can provide both linearisable operations and responses to every request while the node remains healthy
options.explanation: Correct. There is no inter-replica partition, but the API and concurrency control must still implement linearizability. The node is also a single point of failure.

options.text: A system choosing consistency during partitions can still achieve 99.99% availability in practice
options.explanation: Correct. CAP availability requires *every* non-failing node to respond. Quorum systems refuse only on the minority side, and partitions are rare, so measured availability can be very high (Spanner targets 99.999%).

options.text: PACELC's 'else' branch says that, without partitions, stronger consistency typically costs latency
options.explanation: Correct. Coordinating replicas (quorum writes, leader reads) requires extra round trips, which is the everyday cost of consistency.

options.text: If a system isn't linearisable, it must be CAP-available
options.explanation: Incorrect. Many systems are neither. For example, a leader-follower database with async replication isn't linearisable (stale follower reads) and also refuses writes when followers can't reach the leader.

options.text: CAP lets you trade a little consistency for a little availability continuously
options.explanation: Incorrect. CAP is a binary impossibility result about linearisability and total availability. Continuous trade-offs (bounded staleness, quorum sizes) exist, but they're outside what CAP itself describes.

questions.workedExample:
Test each claim against the precise definitions:

- C means linearisable; A means every non-failing node responds; P means the network may lose arbitrary messages.

1. Single node: C and A can coexist with an appropriate implementation; neither follows solely from having one node. True as qualified.
2. CP + high availability: CAP-A is all-or-nothing per node; operational availability is measured over requests. True.
3. PACELC else-branch: true by definition.
4. Non-linearisable ⇒ available? No; async leader-follower is a counterexample.
5. CAP is binary, not a dial. False.

link.title: CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer, InfoQ)

questions.prompt: Replicas run in two distant regions. Writes must be linearisable, and every acknowledged write must survive destruction of either region. Why can writes not simply acknowledge after a local-only update?

options.text: A local update proves both regions hold durable copies
options.explanation: Incorrect. The remote region may not have received the write yet.

options.text: The write needs a durable copy in another region before acknowledgement, so confirmation adds cross-region delay
options.explanation: Correct. Surviving loss of the accepting region requires the other region to hold the acknowledged data.

options.text: One-way transmission without confirmation proves remote durability
options.explanation: Incorrect. Sending a message alone does not establish that the remote copy is durable.

options.text: Linearisability makes physical replication unnecessary
options.explanation: Incorrect. Ordering guarantees do not themselves preserve data after a whole region is destroyed.

questions.workedExample: Separate operation ordering from survival. A local acknowledgement before remote persistence risks losing that acknowledged write if the local region is destroyed. Waiting for remote confirmation pays the network journey and remote work. A design preserving consistency must refuse unsafe operations when coordination is unavailable; its quorum placement and recovery policy determine which failures it can continue through.

link.title: Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (Abadi, PDF)

questions.prompt: A global profile service has its primary database in Virginia and an asynchronous read replica in Sydney. Sydney users read locally (~5 ms) instead of from Virginia (~200 ms round trip). Which PACELC choice is this, and what anomaly must you handle?

options.text: PC: during partitions the replica refuses reads
options.explanation: Incorrect. The scenario is about normal operation, with no partition, and an async replica would usually keep serving (stale) reads during a partition anyway.

options.text: EC: users always see their latest update
options.explanation: Incorrect. Reading from an asynchronous replica is the opposite of choosing consistency. Recent writes may not have arrived yet.

options.text: EL: a user may not see their own edit immediately after saving it, so you need read-your-writes handling
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing local reads trades consistency for latency. The classic fix is to route a user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write, or to read from the replica only once it has caught up to the user's last write position.

options.text: Both linearisable and CAP-available, because there is only one primary
options.explanation: Incorrect. One primary does not make asynchronous follower reads linearisable or remove network partitions. This scenario concerns stale local reads during normal operation, which is the else branch of PACELC.

questions.workedExample:
No partition is involved, so this is the **E** branch: latency versus consistency.

```
local read:   ~5 ms, maybe stale
primary read: ~200 ms, fresh
```

The painful anomaly is a user editing their profile, being redirected to the profile page and seeing the old version. Read-your-writes options:

- After a write, pin reads to the primary until the replica has caught up; a fixed 10-second pin is only a heuristic and cannot guarantee read-your-writes.
- Record the write's log position; read from the replica only once it has replayed past it.

Everyone else's reads can stay local and fast.

lessons.title: Describe actual read guarantees and quorum overlap
lessons.summary: Use Cassandra and ZooKeeper to distinguish quorum intersection, freshness and linearisability.
lessons.body:
PACELC classifications summarise choices, but a concrete operation needs a concrete guarantee. Replica counts and read behaviour explain why two systems with the same broad label can expose different values.

## Concrete read guarantees

- **Cassandra** with `ONE` reads and writes favours availability and low latency when at least one actual replica for the key is reachable, but can still time out or reject requests. With `QUORUM` reads and writes, it pays latency for stronger guarantees (though it still isn't fully linearisable without lightweight transactions). The rule behind this, quorum overlap, is worked through below.

- **etcd** serves linearisable reads by default, confirming with a quorum before answering. **ZooKeeper** commits writes through a quorum, but by default a client reads from whichever server it's connected to, which may lag: reads are ordered but can be stale. `sync()` is a useful freshness barrier, but is not a quorum operation and is not a strict linearisability guarantee under all failures. Same "CP" label, different everyday guarantee.

## Quorum overlap

In a leaderless store like Cassandra, each key is copied to several replicas. A write is reported successful once some of them acknowledge it, and a read asks some of them and takes the newest answer. For a completed write and a subsequent read over the same fixed replica set, the groups must overlap when their combined replica counts exceed the number of replicas. This is an intersection guarantee; timestamps, concurrent updates and partially applied writes still affect which value is returned.

```formula reference
W + R > N
Q = ⌊N / 2⌋ + 1
where
N: number of replicas for the key in the fixed replica set
W: number of replicas acknowledging the completed write
R: number of replicas consulted by the subsequent read
Q: number in a majority quorum
⌊ ⌋: floor, rounding down to a whole number
>: is greater than
In words: read and write groups must overlap if their combined sizes exceed the replica count. Majority reads and writes force that intersection, but intersection alone is not linearisability.
```

With three replicas, `QUORUM` reads and writes each require two, so every read group intersects every successful write group. `ONE` reads and writes can use different replicas and miss an update. Overlap is necessary but not sufficient for linearisability: concurrent writes, last-write-wins timestamps and failed writes that partly landed still need extra machinery such as lightweight transactions.

> [!tip] The everyday question
> PACELC's "E" half is the one you face daily. Partitions are rare; latency is paid on every request. "Do we need this read to be strongly consistent, at the cost of a cross-zone round trip?" is a question you'll ask constantly.

## Key takeaways
- Describe each API’s guarantees rather than relying on a CP or AP label.
- Read and write replica counts exceeding the replication factor force overlap under the model’s assumptions.
- Overlap alone does not provide linearisability in the presence of concurrent or partly applied writes.
- ZooKeeper follower reads may lag committed writes; etcd’s default linearisable reads use a different contract.

## Further reading
- [Please stop calling databases CP or AP](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html)
- [Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)
- [ZooKeeper consistency guarantees](https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/current/zookeeperProgrammers.html#ch_zkGuarantees)
- [etcd API guarantees](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/api_guarantees/)
- [ZooKeeper sync quorum discussion](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ZOOKEEPER-1675)

questions.prompt: A Cassandra key has three replicas. Consider a completed write followed by a read over that same fixed replica set, with no concurrent updates. Which combinations force the read replica group to overlap the write acknowledgement group? Select all that apply.

options.text: Write `QUORUM`, read `QUORUM`
options.explanation: Correct. Any group of two replicas must share at least one member with any other group of two from this same three-replica set.

options.text: Write `ONE`, read `ONE`
options.explanation: Incorrect. The writer can acknowledge on one replica while the reader consults a different one.

options.text: Write `ALL`, read `ONE`
options.explanation: Correct. If all three acknowledged the write, a read from any one shares a member with that group. Requiring every replica also makes writes unavailable when one cannot acknowledge.

options.text: Write `ONE`, read `QUORUM`
options.explanation: Incorrect. The write may acknowledge on the one replica that the two-replica read skips.

options.text: Write `QUORUM`, read `ONE`
options.explanation: Incorrect. A single-replica read can choose the replica absent from the two-replica write acknowledgement group.

questions.workedExample: Label the replicas A, B and C. A write acknowledged by A and B intersects either A/B, A/C or B/C: every two-replica read contains A or B. A single-replica read can choose C and miss that acknowledgement group. This establishes intersection only. Cassandra's timestamp reconciliation, concurrent updates and partially applied writes mean overlap alone does not establish linearisability; lightweight transactions provide additional coordination.

questions.prompt: Service A updates a feature flag in ZooKeeper and then sends Service B a message saying "flag updated". Service B, connected to a different ZooKeeper server, reads the flag and sees the **old** value. ZooKeeper is usually called CP. What's going on?

options.text: ZooKeeper has lost the write because of a partition
options.explanation: Incorrect. The write was committed by a quorum before A was told it succeeded. It isn't lost; B's server simply hasn't applied it yet.

options.text: ZooKeeper reads can lag; B should require at least the version A observed, waiting until it is visible
options.explanation: Correct. A follower read can be stale. Passing A's version lets B reject older results. sync() improves freshness but is not a strict guarantee under all failures because it is not a quorum operation.

options.text: This can't happen in a CP system, so there must be a bug
options.explanation: Incorrect. A 'CP' label says how a system behaves during a partition. It doesn't promise every read is linearisable in normal operation. That's exactly why the lesson says to describe actual guarantees.

options.text: Service B's clock is behind Service A's
options.explanation: Incorrect. ZooKeeper orders updates with its own transaction IDs, not client wall clocks. The issue is replication lag on B's server.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the events:

```
1. A -> leader: set flag=on
2. quorum commits, A gets OK
3. A -> B: "flag updated"
4. B -> follower F: get flag
5. F hasn't applied step 2 yet
   -> returns flag=off
```

The message in step 3 travels outside ZooKeeper, so ZooKeeper's per-client ordering doesn't cover it. Fix: A includes the version number so B can wait for at least that version. A preceding `sync()` alone is not a strict linearisability guarantee under all failures.

Lesson: two systems both labelled CP can have very different read guarantees. That's the E branch of PACELC at work.

lessons.title: Make a consistency decision explicit
lessons.summary: State the gain, cost, acceptable business behaviour and assumptions behind a choice of consistency.
lessons.body:
Every interesting design decision gives something up. Senior engineers aren't distinguished by knowing the "right" technology. They're distinguished by naming what each option costs, quantifying it where possible, and matching it to the requirements.

This lesson collects the trade-offs you'll meet again and again in later modules.

## A template for any decision

When you choose between options, say these four things out loud:

1. **What we gain.** "Reads are served from local replicas in ~2 ms."
2. **What we give up.** "Reads may be up to 1 s stale."
3. **Why that's acceptable here.** "Product prices change rarely; checkout re-reads from the primary."
4. **What would change our mind.** "If we add live auctions, staleness becomes unacceptable."

Point 4 is often skipped and is the most valuable. It records the assumption the design depends on.

## Consistency vs availability (and latency)

The earlier CAP and PACELC units established this trade-off. In practice it appears as a spectrum:

```
 stronger                      weaker
 consistency                   consistency
 <------------------------------------->
 linearisable  causal  read-your  eventual
               writes
 coordination                 fewer read
 may add latency              coordination
                              waits
```

The diagram is only a rough trade-off sketch: weaker consistency does not guarantee faster responses or availability, and consistency models are not all points on a single total order.

How to choose:

| Data | Typical choice |
|---|---|
| Account balance, stock | Strong |
| Username uniqueness | Strong |
| User's own profile edits | Read-your-writes |
| Like counts, view counts | Eventual |
| Recommendations | Eventual, even stale |

> [!tip] Mix within one system
> Most real systems use strong consistency for a small core of critical data and weaker models for everything else. An e-commerce site might serve the catalogue from a cache that's minutes stale, but decrement inventory with a transactional conditional write.

## Key takeaways
- State what an option gains, what it gives up, why that is acceptable and what would change your mind.
- Money, inventory and uniqueness need authoritative decisions; counts and recommendations often permit staleness.
- Consistency models do not form a simple speed guarantee; match the actual contract to each data type.

## Further reading
- [Eventually Consistent (Werner Vogels)](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html)
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

questions.prompt: Which piece of data most clearly needs **strong** consistency?

options.text: The number of likes on a post
options.explanation: Incorrect. If a like count is a few seconds behind, nobody is harmed. Counts are a classic case for eventual consistency.

options.text: The remaining quantity of a limited-edition item at checkout
options.explanation: Correct. If two buyers both read 'one left' from stale replicas and both succeed, you oversell. Decrementing inventory needs a transactional or conditional write against a single source of truth.

options.text: A personalised 'recommended for you' list
options.explanation: Incorrect. Recommendations can be minutes or hours stale without any user noticing. Strong consistency would add cost for no benefit.

options.text: The view count on a video
options.explanation: Incorrect. View counts are often approximate and aggregated asynchronously (YouTube's counts famously lag). Eventual consistency is fine.

questions.workedExample:
Ask: *what goes wrong if a reader sees a stale value?*

| Data | Harm from staleness |
|---|---|
| Like count | Number slightly off |
| Recommendations | Slightly less relevant |
| Inventory at checkout | Oversold item, refunds, angry customer |
| View count | Number slightly off |

For this ordinary shopping example, inventory has the clearest immediate correctness requirement; count and recommendation freshness can also matter under other business rules. Implement it with e.g. `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0` and check the affected row count.

lessons.title: Trade write acknowledgement latency against loss risk
lessons.summary: Compare PostgreSQL, Kafka and Redis acknowledgement controls, then use batching to share flush costs.
lessons.body:
A successful write response makes a promise. Decide whether it means an in-memory update, a durable local flush or a required replicated commit, then account for the latency of keeping that promise.

## Latency vs durability

When is a write "done"? The earlier you acknowledge it, the faster it is and the more you can lose.

| Acknowledge after... | Additional work | Remaining loss risks |
|---|---|---|
| Written to process memory | Memory update | Process or machine failure before persistence |
| Written to OS page cache | Kernel write | OS crash or power loss before persistence |
| fsync to local durable storage | Storage flush | Storage failure, corruption or later logical deletion |
| Durably replicated to a second zone | Replication acknowledgement | Loss of required durable copies, common failures or logical deletion |
| Durably replicated across regions | Cross-region acknowledgement | Protocol/storage failures, loss of required copies or logical deletion |

> [!note] Content gap: generic durability latency figures
> Exact latency ranges are omitted because no representative measurements support them. Replication is not itself a promise that remote copies are durably flushed; verify the acknowledgement contract and failure model.

Real knobs that control this:

- **Postgres** `synchronous_commit`: the default `on` waits for the WAL to be flushed locally (and, if synchronous standbys are configured, on them too). `off` acknowledges before the flush; a crash can lose up to about three times `wal_writer_delay` of commits (around 600 ms with the 200 ms default), but never corrupts the database. `remote_apply` waits until a synchronous standby has *applied* the commit, so reads there see it. It can be set per transaction.
- **Kafka** producer `acks`: `0` (fire and forget), `1` (leader only), `all` (all in-sync replicas), combined with the topic's `min.insync.replicas`. Kafka 3.0 changed the producer defaults to `acks=all` and idempotence on when settings do not conflict. A bug left idempotence off in 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 unless enabled explicitly; fixes shipped in 3.0.1, 3.1.1 and 3.2.0. `min.insync.replicas` defaults to 1; a value such as 2 with at least 3 appropriately placed replicas improves tolerance of one replica loss, but no setting alone guarantees zero loss under all failures.
- **Redis** persistence: no persistence, RDB snapshots (lose everything since the last snapshot), or the append-only file (AOF) with `appendfsync always` (slow, safest), `everysec` (the usual choice: lose about a second of writes) or `no` (let the OS decide when to flush).

Batching (group commit) softens this trade-off: fsync once for many writes. A log that does one fsync at a time can only do so many per second, and each one can make a whole batch durable:

For an illustrative log whose flush takes 2 ms, serial one-commit flushes allow about 500 commits/s. If each flush makes 50 commits durable, that same flush capacity can cover about 25,000 commits/s. The improvement comes from sharing the expensive flush, rather than weakening the durability acknowledgement.

These illustrative ceilings assume flushes happen one after another and that there are always enough commits waiting to fill a batch. The price is latency: a commit may wait for the next batch, by an amount set by the batching policy, queueing and flush completion time. Kafka and most databases do this, which is why throughput can be high even with durable writes.

## Throughput vs latency

Batching, buffering and compression can improve throughput while adding waiting or CPU work. End-to-end latency can still improve if they reduce a bottleneck:

- Kafka's `linger.ms` can wait to fill an incomplete batch, reducing per-request overhead; measure whether that improves throughput for the workload. Recent versions default it to 5 ms (it was 0 before Kafka 4.0); high-volume producers often raise it further.
- Nagle's algorithm in TCP delays small packets to coalesce them (often disabled with `TCP_NODELAY` for interactive traffic).
- Running servers at high utilisation is cheaper but increases queueing latency, as the latency lesson showed.

## Key takeaways
- The acknowledgement contract determines which crash and storage failures may lose a successful write.
- PostgreSQL commit settings, Kafka acknowledgement and ISR settings, and Redis persistence choices need explicit failure models.
- Group commit shares flush costs across a batch, while batching policy can add per-item waiting.
- Replicated data is not automatically durably flushed, and no single setting covers every failure.

## Further reading
- [Asynchronous commit (PostgreSQL)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-async-commit.html)
- [Redis persistence](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/)
- [Kafka producer configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/40/configuration/producer-configs/)
- [Kafka historical default changes](https://kafka.apache.org/34/getting-started/upgrade/)
- [Kafka topic durability configuration](https://kafka.apache.org/40/configuration/topic-level-configs/)

questions.prompt: A team sets Postgres `synchronous_commit = off` to speed up writes. What's the risk?

options.text: A crash can lose the most recently acknowledged transactions (a fraction of a second's worth)
options.explanation: Correct. Commits are acknowledged before the WAL is flushed to disk. If the server crashes, transactions in that window (up to about 3× `wal_writer_delay`, ~600 ms by default) are lost even though clients were told they succeeded.

options.text: The database may become corrupted after a crash
options.explanation: Incorrect. Postgres docs are explicit: asynchronous commit doesn't risk corruption. The WAL is still written in order; only the most recent commits may be missing.

options.text: Reads will return stale data
options.explanation: Incorrect. This setting affects when commits are acknowledged relative to disk flushing, not what readers on the same server see.

options.text: Writes will be rejected when the disk is busy
options.explanation: Incorrect. The opposite: writes are acknowledged sooner because they don't wait on the disk flush.

questions.workedExample: Follow the acknowledgement. With synchronous commit, the normal local durability promise waits for the WAL flush. With asynchronous commit, the client can receive success before that flush. A crash in between may therefore remove recently acknowledged transactions without corrupting the database. PostgreSQL documents an exposure window up to three times wal_writer_delay, around 600 ms with its 200 ms default. Use this only where that loss is acceptable; it can be chosen per transaction.

questions.prompt: A Kafka producer for payment events uses `acks=1`. The topic has replication factor 3. What failure can lose an acknowledged event, and what's the fix?

options.text: Nothing can lose it; replication factor 3 guarantees three copies
options.explanation: Incorrect. Replication factor says how many replicas exist eventually. With `acks=1`, the producer is acknowledged as soon as the leader writes it, before followers have copied it.

options.text: A consumer crash; fix by increasing the number of partitions
options.explanation: Incorrect. Consumer crashes don't delete data from Kafka; the consumer resumes from its committed offset. Partition count affects parallelism, not durability.

options.text: The leader crashes after acknowledging but before followers replicate; fix with `acks=all` and `min.insync.replicas=2`
options.explanation: Correct. A follower that hadn't yet copied the event becomes leader, and the event is gone. `acks=all` waits for all in-sync replicas, and `min.insync.replicas=2` ensures at least two copies exist before the ack, at the cost of slightly higher latency.

options.text: A network partition between producer and broker; fix with `acks=0`
options.explanation: Incorrect. `acks=0` is less durable: the producer doesn't wait for any acknowledgement, so it can't even know a write failed.

questions.workedExample:
Sequence with `acks=1`:

1. Producer sends event E to the leader (broker 1).
2. Broker 1 appends E and acks.
3. Broker 1 crashes before brokers 2 and 3 fetch E.
4. Broker 2 becomes leader without E. **E is lost**, though the producer believes it succeeded.

With `acks=all` + `min.insync.replicas=2`:

- The leader acks only after E is on at least 2 in-sync replicas.
- Losing any one broker still leaves a copy.
- Cost: waiting for replication, with latency determined by placement and load. If fewer than 2 replicas are in sync, writes are rejected. Replicated acknowledgement is not a guarantee that every copy was synchronously flushed to durable media.

Note: since Kafka 3.0 the producer defaults to `acks=all`, so `acks=1` here is an explicit choice someone made for speed. `min.insync.replicas` still defaults to 1 and must be raised on the topic.

questions.prompt: A Redis instance used as a job store has AOF persistence with `appendfsync everysec`. The server loses power. What loss window is normally associated with this setting, assuming healthy storage and normal background flushing?

options.text: No data is lost, because every write is in the append-only file
options.explanation: Incorrect. Writes reach the AOF via the OS page cache. With `everysec`, they are only forced to disk about once a second, so the unflushed tail is lost on power failure.

options.text: Everything since the last RDB snapshot is lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. That's the risk with RDB-only persistence. With AOF on, recovery replays the log up to its last flushed point.

options.text: Roughly the last second of writes is lost
options.explanation: Correct. `everysec` fsyncs about once a second, which is the usual compromise: near-`no` speed with roughly a second of exposure in normal operation. Delayed flushes, disk stalls and persistence settings mean this is not a strict worst-case bound.

options.text: The AOF is corrupted and the whole dataset is lost
options.explanation: Incorrect. A truncated final command can occur, but Redis can load a truncated AOF (dropping the incomplete tail) or repair it with `redis-check-aof`. You lose the tail, not the dataset.

questions.workedExample:
Map the knob to the lesson's durability table:

| `appendfsync` | Flushed | Exposure |
|---|---|---|
| `always` | Every write | ~None |
| `everysec` | ~1/s | ~1 s |
| `no` | When OS decides | OS- and workload-dependent; no Redis one-second bound |

For a job store, ask whether the producer durably tracks and can re-enqueue lost jobs. Idempotent processing helps with duplicate retries; it cannot recover a job that was lost. If this loss window is unacceptable, use `always` (and accept the latency) or a store designed for durable queues.

questions.prompt: A database must flush its log before acknowledging commits. How can group commit improve throughput without weakening that requirement?

options.text: Make one flush durable for several commits, acknowledging them only after it completes
options.explanation: Correct. Several commits share the expensive flush while retaining the required acknowledgement order.

options.text: Acknowledge every commit before flushing and call it a batch
options.explanation: Incorrect. That changes the durability promise rather than implementing durable group commit.

options.text: Skip all future flushes once the first batch succeeds
options.explanation: Incorrect. Later commits still need their data persisted before acknowledgement.

options.text: Guarantee zero waiting regardless of the batch trigger
options.explanation: Incorrect. A commit may wait for batching, queueing and flush completion.

questions.workedExample: Compare the work per flush. One-at-a-time commit gives each flush to one transaction; group commit lets one completed flush cover several. Every covered commit still waits for durable completion. The throughput gain depends on enough waiting work and the rest of the system; batching policy may add latency.

questions.prompt: A Kafka producer sending many small messages raises `linger.ms` from 5 to 50. What is the main trade-off?

options.text: Messages become less durable
options.explanation: Incorrect. Durability is governed by `acks` and replication, not by how long the producer waits to fill a batch.

options.text: Consumers must poll less often
options.explanation: Incorrect. `linger.ms` is a producer setting; it doesn't change how consumers poll.

options.text: Throughput falls because the producer waits
options.explanation: Incorrect. Waiting can improve throughput by filling batches, but the benefit depends on traffic, batch size and the existing bottleneck.

options.text: Potentially larger, more efficient batches, at the cost of extra waiting before a batch is sent
options.explanation: Correct. A larger linger setting can amortise request overhead and improve compression. A full batch can send sooner, and backpressure or broker delay can add waiting beyond the linger timer.

questions.workedExample: The timer controls how long the producer may wait to collect more records before sending an incomplete batch. A higher setting gives more opportunity to share overhead, but a latency-sensitive message may wait longer. The batch can send sooner when full, and actual latency also includes queueing, backpressure, transmission and broker processing. Measure whether batching helps the real bottleneck before increasing the setting.

lessons.title: Price availability and data movement
lessons.summary: Compare the cost of downtime with resilience spending, and account for transfer, storage and idle headroom.
lessons.body:
Technical resilience and cloud usage both consume a budget. Make the assumptions visible so a design review can compare the cost of the system with the cost of its failure.

## Cost

Cost is a first-class requirement, not an afterthought.

- **Each nine is expensive.** Going from 99.9% to 99.99% often means multi-zone everything, automated failover and on-call staffing. Ask what an hour of downtime actually costs the business.
- **Data transfer adds up.** Some cross-zone and internet egress traffic is charged per GB; routes, service exceptions and free allowances vary by provider. A chatty cross-zone microservice architecture can cost more in transfer than in compute. Zone-aware routing (prefer a same-zone replica), compression and consumers that fetch from the nearest replica all cut the bill.
- **Storage tiers.** Hot SSD, object storage and archive tiers have different storage, request and retrieval prices; compare current provider pricing for the expected workload. Lifecycle policies move cold data down.
- **Over-provisioning vs autoscaling.** Headroom costs money; too little costs outages.

To price a time-based availability target, combine its downtime allowance with an explicit cost per hour. A request-based target needs a model of affected requests and their impact.

This is a **budget scenario**, not a prediction that the service will use every minute it is allowed. Compare the plausible reduction in downtime losses with the full extra infrastructure, staffing and operational cost. Include contractual and reputational consequences when they matter.

> [!example] Pricing the trade-off
> Suppose an outage costs £20k per hour. 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours a year (about £175k of downtime cost if you use the whole budget); 99.99% allows about 53 minutes (about £18k). The upgrade saves roughly £157k a year. If moving to 99.99% costs £300k/year in extra infrastructure and staff, it isn't worth it on these numbers, unless downtime also causes reputational or regulatory damage.

## Key takeaways
- An availability target is a business choice: compare additional infrastructure and staffing with the downtime risk it reduces.
- Cross-zone and internet traffic, retrieval prices and spare capacity can dominate costs.
- The downtime-budget calculation is a scenario, not a forecast that the full budget will actually be used.

## Further reading
- [AWS Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)
- [Embracing Risk (Google SRE)](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/)
- [Magic Pocket (Dropbox)](https://dropbox.tech/infrastructure/magic-pocket-infrastructure)

questions.prompt: A resilience proposal costs more each year than the estimated direct downtime losses it avoids. What is the soundest decision process?

options.text: Approve it because an extra nine always pays for itself
options.explanation: Incorrect. There is no universal financial return for a stricter availability target.

options.text: Reject it without checking what the downtime estimate omits
options.explanation: Incorrect. Contracts, reputation, customer harm and regulatory impact may change the decision.

options.text: Treat the target's entire downtime budget as a certain future loss
options.explanation: Incorrect. A budget scenario is not a forecast of actual incidents.

options.text: Review the full business impact, uncertainty and cheaper recovery options before deciding
options.explanation: Correct. Compare total costs and benefits under explicit assumptions rather than treating either the target or a narrow revenue model as decisive.

questions.workedExample: Start with the stated direct comparison: those savings alone do not justify the extra cost. Then check omitted consequences and uncertainty, the likelihood and shape of failures, and alternatives such as faster recovery. Record why the chosen target fits the business and what evidence would change it.

questions.prompt: Your cloud bill shows cross-zone data transfer costing more than compute. Services run in 3 zones. Which changes would **reduce** cross-zone traffic? Select all that apply.

options.text: Zone-aware routing, so callers prefer an instance of the next service in their own zone
options.explanation: Correct. Preferring same-zone destinations can reduce cross-zone calls when local capacity exists, while retaining fallback to other zones.

options.text: Compressing large request and response payloads between services
options.explanation: Correct. Transfer is billed per GB, so fewer bytes means a smaller bill, for a little CPU.

options.text: Letting Kafka consumers fetch from a replica in their own zone instead of always from the leader
options.explanation: Correct. Kafka supports follower fetching (rack-aware replica selection). Consumers in other zones no longer pull every byte across zones from the leader.

options.text: Splitting each service into several smaller services spread across all zones
options.explanation: Incorrect. More services means more network hops, each of which may cross zones. This usually increases transfer costs.

options.text: Adding a synchronous replica of every database in each zone
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each write is now copied to the other zones, adding cross-zone traffic. It may be worth it for durability, but it doesn't cut the bill.

questions.workedExample: Trace where bytes cross zone boundaries. Local routing can avoid a crossing, compression can reduce crossing bytes, and eligible replica fetching can keep consumer reads local. More service hops and additional replication add traffic. Verify the provider's charging rules and Kafka's replica-selection configuration. Local preference needs fallback and load-balancing safeguards when a zone is busy or unavailable.
